speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. I desire to direct the attention of this house to an address purporting to have been delivered last evening in this capital city by a man named W. D. Herridge, and published in a newspaper known as the Ottawa Citizen, a paper to whose subversive activities it was necessary for this house to refer yesterday. I shall explain in a moment my question of privilege. Let me say, sir, that it affects the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) and his entire group, the Prime Minister of Can-' ada (Mr. Mackenzie King) and our entire group, the leaders of the other two groups opposite, and every one of the 245 members of the House of Commons.
This newspaper contains what purports to be a verbatim report of the speech, and among other things this gentleman said this:
The first thing that Canadians have to do is to give their country a free parliament. Because to-day the parliament of Canada is not free to serve the people.
The second vile slur he cast upon this parliament and every member thereof is contained in this language:
You must choose between the old parties and democracy. If the old parties are left in control of parliament, I believe they will unite. After the next election, or perhaps before-
That affects the members of this house.
-the Liberal and Conservative parties will become one party. Its government, in name, will be a national government. In fact, it will be a fascist government.
Those are ugly words in Canada to-day. Lest there should be any doubt as to his charge of conspiracy-

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. SLAGHT ADDRESS DELIVERED BY HON. W. D. HERRIDGE IN OTTAWA ON MARCH 1

If my hon. friend will bear me out in this matter of grave importance, I believe he will agree with me in what I propose.
So that he might leave no doubt in the minds of the people of Canada that he was charging conspiracy of a criminal type and character, he used this further language:
When this conspiracy for national government is a little more advanced, the element of crisis will be introduced. There will be a good deal of imperial flag waving. Elder statesmen will be uncorked to take their part in it, little understanding that their venerable voices will be urging empire destroying practices.
That indicates to me, Mr. Speaker, that this gentleman, a new found Moses in his own eyes, a gentleman who is in my view a political mountebank, has charged every member of the House of Commons with being ready to conspire to form a fascist government. He has said that every member of the House of Commons is serving here not in a free parliament, and he abuses all parties and groups alike.
My friend who interrupted will find that he is taken care of in the course of the address. I quote further:
This is not the proper time to deal with that or refer to it.

Let me ask this house whether there is a greater patronage monger in the Dominion of Canada than W. D. Herridge. He joined the Conservative party in 1930 for the first time, and he was a fast worker. speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this resolution is to precede the introduction of a bill which will be similar to the one which went through this house last session, and which could not be adopted in the other place because of alleged lack of time. The legislation had been introduced only at the end of the session because the report of the commission did not come in until after the Easter recess. I suggest that I should be allowed to introduce the bill, and if any hon. member wants details, they can be discussed when the bill is before the house. It will be the Penitentiary Act substantially as it is today in the statute, except that it provides for the establishment of a commission of three to replace the superintendent of penitentiaries; the inspectors become assistant commissioners; and in the various sections of the act where the word "superintendent" has to be replaced by "commission" the necessary amendments are provided for.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, under this resolution the responsibility for the solving of this problem is on the government of the day, and not on the opposition. Four years ago this matter came up in the elections and in this house. When the present government was returned four years ago it appointed a royal commission, which toured the world and made its report late last session. The matter went to the senate, and the bill was laid over because, they said, they had not sufficient time to deal with it.

This social and domestic problem is probably one of the most important of our national problems. Just recently the minister's department issued a blue-book containing prison statistics and showing how large is the number of young people who are in these institutions owing to the failure of parliament to help solve the economic problems of unemployment and many other domestic problems. These young people are roaming the country; many of them are high school students who have never before been in such institutions. Some are sent to the county gaols for vagrancy, and then escape, and finally they land up in the federal institutions. I invite attention to the figures concerning these young people to be found in part II of the departmental statistics recently issued in blue-book form by the bureau of statistics. The number of young people in these institutions, many of them through no fault of their own, is surprising. Here one sees the cause and effect of unemployment in this country.
In England about half of these institutions have been closed. They have learned modem ways of prison reform. I have here reports which were made by the secretary of state for the home department in Great Britain, where they have been investigating this problem for the last four years in numerous ways. Here are four government books dealing with this matter. One has to do with the problem of youth and unemployment. Another relates to summary jurisdiction reform concerning the non-payment of fines and other sums of money, because in Canada there is still imprisonment for debt. The report shows that a large number of people were sent to these institutions because of non-payment of debt, and that some of them were put there without bail-an evil which was supposed to have been abolished years ago. Here is another report of an interdepartmental committee in Great Britain on the employment of prisoners inside and outside the institution, the care of their families, prison reform on a large scale, and the Borstal system. Why do we not do something? There is a national service program for youth in England; why not here?
As regards those who suffer through the delinquencies of persistent offenders, the wives and children at home, what have we done to meet the problem of taking care of these unfortunate people? Absolutely nothing. I pass one of these institutions in the train every week-I refer to the one at Collin's Bay-and I have been wondering what steps have been taken to improve conditions there. I do not blame the present

Penitentiaries Commission
minister at all. He is a humane man and like his predecessors, has done the best he can to better the conditions that exist in our federal penal institutions. The responsibility is not altogether on the minister; it is very largely on this parliament. This is a problem that must be dealt with.
I suggest that those who sit in the chamber at the other end of this building should have some work to do. If they followed the practice in the senate at Washington they would be up and doing and not on holidays all the time. They are the body that threw out the bill last year and they should be here now to deal with this matter. Why are they on holiday? They can find lots of work here. It seems to me they should be studying this problem. I should like to see the bill introduced over there first.
We find in the provincial institutions the same state of affairs that exists under the federal department. There is also there an enormous increase among those who are classed as youths. We have had no results from the $4,000,000 spent since 1900 on commissions appointed to deal with various national problems. I am opposed to the appointing of any more such commissions. As I say, the responsibility is on the minister and on parliament. I have faith in the minister and I believe that he would administer the affairs of his department in a very satisfactory manner if he were given a free hand. I have no doubt that he could get along very well without commissions. It is a social, not a political question, of real importance.
Owing to the increase in the number of inmates some of the institutions in the province are overcrowded, with the result that last month, in the depth of winter, 131 men had to be taken by train from Portsmouth to the west, under conditions which should never have been allowed to exist. This is no time for any such policy as that. If the department has not the necessary buildings in the province, then those buildings should be immediately erected. The conditions that are reported in the newspapers-helpless men being shackled and tied to railway seats-are not conducive to law and order. These conditions are subversive of good government; they cause criticism and resentment. It is not fair to the wives and children of these men. If the country can spend $3,500,000 on a federal supreme court building in Ottawa- so far we have spent some $8,000,000 here on new buildings-surely some money can be found to carry out the recommendations contained in the report of a commission that has cost so much.
71492-93J
I believe that the minister himself would have carried out some of the suggested reforms had be been given a free hand, because I have every confidence in him. Most of the reforms could be effected without delay. The minister is the dean of the House of Commons and has taken a great interest in this problem. May I offer him another constructive suggestion. Why is not something done in regard to first offenders who are sent to these institutions? A great many of them are sent there for insufficient cause. For instance, a man was found selling magazines on King street, Toronto, and was picked up and charged with vagrancy. He said to the magistrate, "Do I look like a vagrant?" The magistrate replied brusquely, "Yes, $30." One wonders whether there is any Magna Charta. left. No wonder there are so many such trials in our courts. More care should be taken in appointing magistrates.
It seems to me that there would be fewer men in these institutions if the government took steps to reduce unemployment. The time has come when men should no longer be herded into gaols in Canada as they are to-day. I am surprised that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) is not here, because the problem we are discussing at this moment is largely wrapped up in unemployment. It is simply a matter of cause and effect. As to turning it over to a commission, I suggest that we have had enough of commissions in Canada. We have had a radio commission, a railway commission, a coal commission, and others, and I fail to see how this problem can be solved by passing the buck to a commission, because that body would be largely political. The commissions that have been appointed since confederation have merely prevented the House of Commons from dealing with problems that are thus sidetracked. We have almost entirely divested ourselves of responsibility in this house in respect of many national problems, yet when the reports of these various commissions are submitted they are pigeon-holed.
Is it any wonder that there is a decay of parliament and a decline of the House of Commons? The only branch of government that has increased in popularity in the past thirty years is the crown, as unquestionably it has in the dominions and in the old country; but the decay of the House of Commons is evident all along the line, simply because we.have divested ourselves of authority. High school teachers, clergymen and others have been asking for reforms in our penal institutions; they have urged that the problem be dealt with in a comprehensive national way. I do not subscribe to any of the " sob stuff "
Penitentiaries Commission

that we read in some newspapers on certain aspects of this problem. I believe that the minister wishes to have these institutions conducted in an efficient humane manner for the benefit of the community as a whole and I hope that he will be given a free hand. Men should be trained and equipped for this work. I am sure that some really practicable solution would be found if the minister took the matter into his own hands and had power to act at once. Value would be given us for the money expended. I venture to say that if the minister looked carefully into the records of the first offenders in provincial, municipal and federal institutions, at least one-third of the first offenders would be let out on parole and sent home. I hope this will be done during the royal visit, as has been done in England on different occasions. Certainly some steps should be taken to relieve the congestion by restoring to their families those first offenders who have got into trouble largely through riding the rods, and for less serious infractions of the laws respecting motor cars, petty thefts, escapes, and so on; and this should apply also to minor offenders who reform.

That is more characteristic of him. He says he does not want any more commissions, and I am heartily in accord with that. We have too many commissions in Canada to-day; there is an ever-rising tendency to adopt that form of government. They are expensive; they immediately start to build up a large body of officials under them. These positions are not filled by the civil service commission; they are to all intents and purposes political appointments. That is not so important. What I do say is that this is a ready means of avoiding responsibility. How often have we seen this happen here: we have a grievance concerning some department and the minister in charge, apparently with the best intentions in the world, says, "I am sorry, but that is run by a commission and I am not responsible. I am only the mouthpiece of the commission. I will tell the commission what you say, and if they care to pay attention to it they will do so; if not they will not."
I do not want to see the government lose its responsibility. Why do we not have a commission for each of the fifteen or seventeen portfolios, if we are going to develop along these lines? As the hon. member behind me said, the present Minister of Justice has conducted his department for many years with credit and distinction to himself; his administration of the penitentiaries, the parole board and so on, which I have had some occasion to look into, has been excellent, and the same could be said with regard to the previous minister, Hon. Mr. Guthrie. Then why do we want to get away from that system and put in a commission, certainly not as able as the present minister and more or less political in character? Above all, why should the government evade the responsibility of dealing with the matter? The minister is perfectly capable of handling this branch of his department; why not let him do it? Why not a commission to administer the Post Office Department, which, instead of having only six offices, has hundreds and thousands of post offices to deal with? The Department of Public Works employs far more people and expends a great deal more money than the Department of Justice. Why not put a commission in there?
Since I have been in this house I have noted a growing tendency to appoint commissions of this kind, and with one or two exceptions they have all resulted in lessening the authority and freedom of parliament, about which we heard just a few moments ago from an hon. member on the opposite side. If we continue to hand over our duties and responsibilities

to a commission here and a commission there, soon vve will not be a free parliament; we will be a parliament run by political boards calling themselves commissions. Even if I am the only one to vote against the bill I will oppose it for that reason.

I am not rising to offer any objection to this measure or to criticize the minister' particularly, but I do think there are a few things that should be said. Some of them have been said already, but I should like to add one or two observations.
The resolution before us provides for the establishment of a commission. While we have not the details of the bill before us, from the observations of the minister I gathered that he contemplates only such amendments to the act as will erect a commission which will in turn work out a policy for the improvement of general penitentiary conditions. If I am too restrictive in my definition I wish to be corrected at this stage. If that is the case I think parliament would be evading its responsibility at this time if it did not take cognizance of present day conditions, which are undoubtedly aggravated conditions having in mind misdemeanours by the youth of the country, and lay down at least in theory some principles which would guide this commission in the discharge of its duties. I say that, Mr. Chairman, because if the commission is only to manage the penitentiaries I think we are wasting our time here and, as the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) has said, I would far rather see the penitentiaries remain under the Department of Justice. On the other hand, however, if the duties of the commission include studying the causes of crime and the alarming increase in crime, there may be some justification for its establishment, although I am not too enthusiastic about it even under those conditions.
It appears to me that parliament is taking notice of the congested condition of our penitentiaries and of the much advertised need of some reform in the method of dealing with criminals after they are convicted and incarcerated. That, it seems to me, is what parliament has focused its attention upon to the almost entire exclusion of any consideration of the causes of crime. I have before me a statement by Hon. Leslie Miller, governor of Wyoming, in which there are one or two things to which I think it would be profitable for me to refer and for the committee to hear. This gentleman, obviously recognizing his responsibility, made a careful study of crime in his locality, and he makes this observation:
The essence of criminality is an anti-social attitude on the part of the criminal. This rMr. Neill.]
is something that is acquired slowly, over a period of years. Case histories of thousands of prisoners reveal that invariably the criminal, not counting those imprisoned for crimes of passion, slipped into their criminal habits by degrees, with a long procession of crimes, each progressively worse.
_ This observation is not new but it is pertinent to the present situation. Criminals do not become such in an outburst of passion, except in a minority of cases. They grow out of a procession of habits or practices due largely to condition or environment. If that is true, my point is that parliament will not be properly discharging its duty unless it takes cognizance of that fact and of present day conditions, and at least attempts to make some provision for the correction or prevention of crime rather than merely an improved method of dealing with the criminal after he is created. There is an old adage which says, "Satan finds mischief for idle hands to do." I can remember that from my earliest childhood. The point, of course, is that idleness breeds crime. Of that there can be no doubt.
In the same article there is quoted an eminent French authority on criminology, Henry T. F. Rhodes, professor in the institute of criminology at the university of Lyons, France. He makes this pertinent observation:
It is modern industrial society which produced the modern slum, that worst of all mass-produced articles. We have mass-produced slums and education at the same time.
Then he goes on to point out this fact, which I think also is pertinent, that millions of dollars are spent on improving educational facilities for youth; children are given airy, healthful schoolday surroundings, but they go back from those surroundings to live in the slums. Then he continues with this observation :
They sleep night by night with three or four others in a stifling room. Often the living room is used for sleeping also. But overcrowding does not breed only the stunted and the anaemic. It breeds murder, sexual crimes and other abominations, things which are not mentioned at the public schools or in the homes of the subscribers to charity. The slums, plus an education fitting slum-dwellers for something better in a world which cannot afterwards give it, are the root of this dark problem.
What I .want to emphasize is that parliament ought to recognize that the increase in crime in Canada, as in other countries like the United States, France and Great Britain, is largely due to the economic conditions which have prevailed during the last ten or fifteen years. I should like the minister to give heed to what I am saying.

If the hon. member will direct his question to the minister, he will get accurate information. However, I will hazard the opinion, without having the figures before me, that our penitentiary population has increased during the period of depression. As a matter of fact, during the last ten years crime has become a racket. While this has not been caused solely by the depression, it has been aggravated by it. Crime has become organized in our great cities, as was evidenced by the recent murder in Toronto of a man named Windsor. Crime is an organized racket, but I would go even further and say that it is an organized business. Those at the head of these rackets practise skilful business principles in their administration, and of course use criminal methods to enforce their will. This condition has been aggravated by the unemployment and idleness of so many young people, and it causes me a good deal of alarm. Perhaps later on when the bill has [DOT]been brought down the minister will give us accurate figures for Canada, but the figures for the United States-I am not holding up that country as a horrible example by any means-show that one out of thirty-seven of the population is in the criminal class. I think the percentage is much less in Canada, because we have not the congested areas they have in the United States, but the incident in Toronto, to which I referred, and the other incident in Windsor about six or eight months ago, indicate that this condition has spread into Canada in the same organized form as it has in the United States.
Perhaps the minister will favour the committee with particulars of the ages of our criminals. I again speak from more or less superficial knowledge when I say that the youthfulness of our criminal class is something appalling. I know from observation that there are many very young men in our penitentiaries to-day. It is a startling, an appalling situation, arising largely, although not wholly, out of idleness, out of lack of opportunity to work. Parliament must take cognizance of this phase of the situation. As the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) said a moment ago, the Department of Labour might very well be cooperating with the Department of Justice in an effort to eliminate the economic causes
which lead to crime. These departments should try to present to parliament measures which would serve not only to improve the condition of the criminal after he is convicted but also to prevent the making of criminals through lack of employment and other causes.
It is not my intention to speak in a critical sense. Along with other hon. members I have a good deal of satisfaction in saying that my long acquaintance with the minister has demonstrated to me that he has desired to administer this very difficult matter in a fair, just and I think humane manner. But we dare not disregard the preventive as well as the corrective side of the question.

The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) has objected rather strongly to the appointment of a commission to replace the superintendent of penitentiaries. He says that we have too many commissions and too many officials. But may I say to him-probably he knows this already-that if there is a grievance in that regard, it certainly cannot be directed to the Department of Justice, which is undermanned in every branch. There have been no additions to the staff of the department, although the business has increased tremendously. Whether we call them commissioners or otherwise, these men are certainly needed to do the business which has to be done. This is a very important branch of the administration. I have the following on the authority of the commission which, as the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) has said, made an investigation throughout the world:
In our present system the problem of penal administration is too large in scope and too serious in results to be left in the hands of one man. It is noteworthy, as a matter of record, that Canada is practically the only country where the penal system is not administered by some kind of commission or board.
Then at page 362 of its report, the commission states:
It is of first and immediate importance that legislation should be enacted to make provision for a prison commission.
They have had a prison commission in England since 1877, and they have had a federal prison board in the United States since 1930. As I have stated, the only difference will be that instead of one man there will be three. I can assure my hon. friend that these men will not be selected because of political affiliations. We will try to have men who are expert in this work. It has been urged for some time that there should be a medical man on the staff of the penitentiaries, an expert in mental diseases and that
Penitentiaries Commission

sort of thing. The idea is to have three men at the head of our penal system whose names and abilities will be a guarantee to the people of Canada that this very important branch of the administration is being looked after properly.
The hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) has taken the broader view of the matter. He has said that we should look into the causes of crime and methods of preventing crime and improving social conditions. Of course, penology, which is the subject matter of this bill, is only one branch of criminology, which itself is a branch of sociology, all having to do with human nature. Penology has to do with prison management. I am not sure that my hon. friend's remarks having to do with unemployment and the various temptations that come to young men who are idle, while most appropriate, should not be made part of a different study from that which should be conducted by the heads of penitentiaries. This legislation is to take care of prisoners. Of course the heads of penitentiaries are vitally interested in anything that would tend to cure existing evils and help reform the men committed to their charge, as well as to protect society against them. I assure my hon. friend that I am noting every one of his remarks, and he may be sure that anything that can be considered by the penitentiary commission or the officers of the penitentiary branch in connection with the points he has raised -yvill be most carefully considered. The statistics he has asked for with regard to the age of criminals in Canada and the number of prison inmates in various periods of prosperity and depression I shall be pleased to have prepared and give them to the committee when the subject is up again.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the members of the committee will probably agree with me that the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) is one of the best and most conscientious ministers of justice we have had since confederation, and it is because I am firmly of that opinion, which is generally accepted by the committee, as we have just noticed, that I ask the minister not to insist now upon presenting a bill based upon this resolution.
Everyone knows that the Archambault commission was appointed mostly for sentimental reasons. One of those who advocated its appointment was a very dear friend of mine, a good Canadian and a prominent journalist, the late Harry Anderson, formerly of the Globe of Toronto. It is wrong I believe, to consider penal matters from the point of 
view of sentiment. Gaol should not be made too attractive, although undoubtedly prisoners should be treated not only with justice but with humanity.
The Archambault commission, as the minister said, travelled throughout the world, mostly like Isaac Laquedem, the wandering Jew. They visited several countries and inspected several penitentiaries in the United States, when they could have got the same information by reading books published by the warden of Sing Sing and by other people.
In the last portion of the report we have twenty pages of bibliography, which means that the members of the commission must have read at least four hundred publications before they produced one. A well known book, My Prison, by Sylvio Pellico, published in Italy at the end of the eighteenth century, before Italy was a fascist country, unfortunately is not included in that list.
There is a reference note at the bottom of page 389 of the royal commission's report which takes away a lot of the credit from the report itself. At the foot of the first page of bibliography appears a reference note and I want the members, if the minister decides to go further with this legislation, to read these twenty pages of bibliography; then I am sure they will wonder whether any member of the commission read all these books. The reference note says:	.
This material is, by no means, a bibliography of penology, nor does it include all the printed material studied by the commission. Much of the reference material studied by the commission has come from private sources and public libraries and is not included here.
This bibliography lists only such books, pamphlets, and other material as is at present in the offices of the commission and which will be available for the use of those who are to be entrusted with the administration of Canadian penal institutions. It is hoped that this collection will form the basis of a reference library on penology and criminology in the offices of the prison commission.
Well, I do not believe any more in penology as understood by these gentlemen than I believe in phrenology and technology. It is a splitting of hairs. Of course phrenology is an interesting science. It is based on the lumps a man has on his head. But penology is a different matter. It is the study of crime. There are detective stories that are very interesting-Sherlock Holmes, for instance. I wonder if the adventures of Sherlock Holmes could worthily be included in the alphabetical list of publications appearing at the end of the commission's report. It is surely more interesting than all the books mentioned there.
Another interesting book which does not appear in the bibliography is one which was

Penitentiaries Commission
written by a man who has given his life to improving the character of youth. I refer to Magistrate McKinley, who lives here in Ottawa. He is a very capable man, and I am surprised that his book, which is a small one, does not appear in this list.
I agree fully with the minister that the penitentiaries branch is one of the most important branches of his department. He said that Canada was one of the few countries in which there is no penology board to look after penitentiaries, and he suggests experts. It has been the practice of the dominion government since I have been a member of parliament that when a commission is created the men who are appointed to it are considered experts, whether they are or not. Judge Archambault was the chairman of the commission. He was a good lawyer. He is an ordinary judge, neither very good nor very bad, just the average, and a jolly good fellow. I suggest to the minister that if it is decided to appoint any other commission he select judges who are superannuated, because they are gentlemen of leisure; so long as they have their wits they can do that work very easily, and without delaying the hearing of cases. There are complaints that many lawyers, because of the lack of judges, have not the opportunity to have their cases heard; and when judges-I mean active judges-are on commissions of this kind it creates trouble in the administration of justice. I should like to see passive or superannuated judges selected to act upon commissions of this kind.
The two experts who were joined with Mr. Justice Archambault were distinguished lawyers -Mr. McRuer of Toronto and Mr. Craig of Winnipeg. I have looked in Who's Who to see what was the peculiar experience of those gentlemen in criminal matters. Both have been for short periods of time crown attorneys, one several years ago and the other lately. They may be good lawyers but they cannot be called penologists. Who is the best penologist? He is a man who has started young in an administrative capacity in the management or supervision of penitentiaries, and who has learned that profession little by little until finally he has become acquainted with the wThole thing. I must congratulate the minister upon having appointed as acting superintendent of penitentiaries Mr. Sauvant, a very modest gentleman who is no less able than modest, and who is doing exceptionally well. I should like him to be appointed superintendent of penitentiaries under the present able Minister of Jutice and he should be given full authority. That is my first suggestion.
When the commission is appointed, its members are regarded as distributors of words which are to be received on a silver tray. These men have the science of the matter on which they are to make suggestions. Of course the government is no more bound than is parliament by any suggestion or any recommendation made by any commissioner or by the three together. That is my humble view. They are experts. If the bill passes, the minister intends to appoint to the commission men whose names and abilities will be a guarantee to the people of Canada. He has some of them already; he has Mr. Sauvant; he has others.
For one reason or another Colonel Piuze, who was a very good appointee as warden of the penitentiary of St. Vincent de Paul, left that position and now is head of the Quebec provincial police.

The deputy warden admitted that he had received tales from prisoners and had accepted them, but he contended that it was his duty to do so. The warden also admitted that in certain instances ne took action against prisoners on the strength ot information conveyed to him bv other prisoners.
And so on. This is very bad if it is true. I take the word of the commissioner on this point, although I candidly confess that I have not read the evidence. It seems to me that if those grave charges are substantiated, the only thing to do is to fire that warden at once and replace him with a man who has never failed to maintain order within a penitentiary.
I am not opposed to government legislation.
I am such a staunch supporter of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) that I will not vote against his resolution, or his bill if he presents one. On the other hand, I adjure him in the name of the principles in which we both believe to abandon the idea of submitting a bill based upon the resolution. We have enough commissions. I am against commissions. I am against commissions on principle and I am against this proposal in particular. If you appoint an investigating commission it is all right provided that those who sit on it do not try to make it a permanent institution in order to ensure jobs for themselves for life. Of course, when someone is appointed temporarily in any capacity-I am speaking from my experience as a member of parliament-he is notified that his job will bo temporary, that it will last six months or one year or two years as the case may be, that it will cease some time; but he is never
(Mr. Pcmliot.]
convinced that it will. He expects it to be everlasting and he expects a superannuation besides. Every member knows that.
Who, therefore, is the nigger in the woodpile? Who has been so insistent upon the commissioners recommending the appointment of a penal commission composed, not of phrenologists, not of technologists, but of penologists? Is not the nigger in the woodpile one of those who received a fabulous amount of money-relatively of course; it is not a million dollars but quite a substantial sum-when the investigating commission was carrying on its work? And then did not the minister-I assume this; I may be all wrong- receive, from anyone who had served on the previous commission, an application for the position of secretary to the new commission? Was anyone who served on the investigating commission recommended by someone else to any member of the government to serve on the managing commission? Since those who were acting as commissioners on the previous commission have read so many books that none of us can digest, are they not by that very fact penologists and therefore entitled to be called as experts on the new administrative commission? I would not be surprised at all, because probably there is no one in Canada who has read that quantity of literature; and I would not be surprised if many of those who have written these books are, not in prison, but in other asylums of peace.
I therefore reiterate my request to the minister not to insist upon this proposal. I tell him in advance that I will not vote against it, but I warn him that we have enough commissions in Canada as a whole. There are many commissions and they become irresponsible bodies. I believe in responsible government. I believe in the old policies of responsible government, in virtue of which the minister is responsible for the expenditure of money under his authority. If the Department of Justice is under-manned, let the minister choose good men, and if in his department there are incompetent men, whoever they are, let him fire them and replace them with good men.
If the charges made by the commission against the warden or the authorities-not only the warden but the officers-of Saskatchewan penitentiary are substantiated, then the only thing to do is to dismiss those who are unworthy of the confidence of the Minister of Justice and replace them with good men. There are good men in Canada. The Minister of Justice is one of them; the acting superintendent of penitentiaries, Mr. Sauvant, is another. There are many of them. But if there are outbreaks in the

Penitentiaries Commission
penitentiary at Kingston and in other places, they are on account of the fact that those in charge were incompetent.
Now, what am I told? What is the rumour?
I want to warn the Minister of Justice about it. I want to tell him what is being said in Kingston, where there is a penitentiary. They say that the commission is only a smoke screen to fire some people and replace them with others. It was said at the time that General Ormond was fired, it was said by no less a man than the leader of the Conservative party in the senate. It is beyond my comprehension, and I do not believe it. But, because the Minister of Justice is thoroughly familiar with his own department, and because he is one of the most brilliant parliamentarians and a good Liberal, he will understand that I do not speak as I do to-day in order to displease him. At times we see that policies are enacted to please someone or to displease someone else. The great mistake is that in pleasing someone, one may do wrong; and one may be right in displeasing somebody else. Therefore in such grave matters as this, the main and, indeed, the only consideration should be not to try to please or to refrain from displeasing, but to do what is right and not to do what is wrong. That is all.
I know the Minister of Justice will not do what is wrong, in order to please anyone or to impart to the commissioners the importance which they believe attaches to them, by agreeing with their report, which only justifies the expenses that were paid to them by the country, but he will do what is right [DOT] and will proceed without instituting a new penitentiaries commission.

(Translation) Mr. Chairman, I avail myself of the opportunity offered by this discussion to make a few suggestions which I believe to be in the interest of the administration of justice.
As St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary is situated in my constituency, I wish to draw the attention of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) to the legitimate claims of the officers of that institution.
The time has come, in my opinion, to change the method of paying the salaries and wages of penitentiary staffs. They should be paid twice a month in the same way as other Canadian civil servants. For many years I have been repeatedly urging that this act of justice be done. In addition, our penitentiary staffs should be granted an eight-hour day, and in the interest of good administration their remuneration should be brought up to a reasonable level having regard to the type of 71492-94J
service performed. Indeed, a recommendation to that effect appears on page 353 of the Royal Commission's report, in the following words:
That the pay of officers be brought up to a reasonable level having regard to the type of service performed.
The Royal Commission also recommends that permanent status be granted to officers having one year of service or more. Indeed, why should penitentiary officers not enjoy the same privileges and the same protection as other civil servants?
Another aspect of penitentiary administration which I desire to emphasize is the important problem of the reformation and rehabilitation of the inmates. The staffs should never lose sight of their all-important mission of promoting the moral restoration of their charges. To rehabilitate without breaking should be the watchword of every penitentiary officer worthy of the name. In the performance of his high functions, the warden should never forget that firmness is often disastrous if it excludes charity and kindness. The combination of these virtues can work wonders with the most refractory convicts. Experience, moderation and sound management will enable our penal institutions to rid themselves forever of false conceptions of authority and achieve the fruitful results which the community is entitled to expect from them.
In closing, I desire to urge upon the committee the necessity of improving the training and education of penitentiary inmates, so that when released they may become useful citizens. The teaching of trades in our penitentiaries cannot be too greatly encouraged. Given capable and active instructors, prisoners will be able to learn carpentry, machine work, blacksmithing, shoe-repairing, clothes-making, binding, printing and numerous other trades which will enable them later on to earn their living respectably. However, I cannot over-estimate the importance of the theoretical and practical teaching of agriculture in penitentiaries. Discharged prisoners who go in for farming will be less likely to return to evil ways. The justice department has already achieved commendable results in the matter of education, training and reformation of prisoners. Some of our penitentiary officers have shown considerable ability in that regard; there is still room for improvement, however, as whatever is human is perfectible. In offering these few suggestions in the interest of penitentiary officers and inmates, I believe I am serving the community and the country.

I should have been well
content to have had this resolution pass upon the explanation of the minister, because when the bill comes down there will then be opportunity to consider it, and also because the proposal is very much like the one we had last year.
I have had some experience in connection with criminals and criminology, and I do not think "criminals"-those convicted-are much worse sinners than those who were too smart to get caught. I do not agree with the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) that crime is due to economic conditions.
I did not say that it was due to economic conditions. I said that present day economic conditions largely contributed to the increase of crime.

I am sorry; I put down the word "due." But I would even say that present economic conditions are not largely the cause of crime. I would quote Judge Hamilton of the juvenile court of the city of Winnipeg, as well as James Mutchmore and James Shaver, social workers in that city. Judge Hamilton said that in sections of Winnipeg where boys and girls were trained in the four-sided life, by Christian leaders, crime was practically absent. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) will bear me out in that, because he knows something of it. Judge Hamilton has given his time and work to the upbuilding of the youth of the city of Winnipeg, in which work he has been very successful.
To me the cure for crime among our youth is organized Christian leadership among our boys and girls, training them in the four-sided life. There are hon. members who say that it is not the business of this house to deal with questions concerning morality and spiritual life. I say that if the cause of crime can be removed by training and Christian leadership, then we should take a hand in it, as I think every hon. member of this house does in one way or another. Therefore I am for Christian and moral rearmament among our boys and girls. I shall have more to say on this later on. I hope this will be the last speech at the present stage.

I rise to protest against any further commissions being appointed by this government. The appointment of commissions has come to be quite a popular mode of evading responsibility that should be taken by members of this house. These commissions have also come to be something of a racket. We find judges coming down from the bench to act as commissioners. I object to that, and I think the people of this country

object. We want to keep our judiciary on a very high plane; they should not be constantly leaving the bench and going out on political investigations. I am sure it detracts not only from their dignity but from the high respect in which they should be held. If commissions are necessary someone other than judges should be appointed. The fees that are charged by lawyers, generally friends of the government, are altogether out of keeping with the value of the services rendered. These commissions are expensive luxuries, and they have not been very successful in finding solutions for the problems that they were appointed to investigate. In the last three years the present government has spent almost one and a quarter million dollars on these commissions, largely in order to evade responsibility that should be taken by this government.
I was surprised to hear my good friend the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) state that he was opposed to the appointment of this commission, as well as that of other commissions. With this I heartily agree, but the hon. member went on to say that even though he was opposed to the appointment of this commission he would support it because his good friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) was introducing the requisite resolution in this house. I do not think it is conducive to the enactment of good legislation when hon. members will speak against a bill and then vote for it.
I rose, Mr. Chairman, only to register my protest against the appointment of any further commissions by this government. I agree with the other speakers who have said that the Minister of Justice himself, with his adequate staff, is quite capable of giving good service to this country in regard to any penitentiary reform that may be necessary.

speechtext: Hon. P. J. A. CARDIN (Minister of Public Works) moved the second reading of Bill No. 25, to authorize an agreement between His Majesty the King and the corporation of the city of Ottawa.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1939
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I inform the house about certain questions in connection with this agreement. Certain criticisms have been made, both inside and outside the house, as to this $100.000 which is to be paid to the city of Ottawa On one occasion an hon. member from one oi

the Winnipeg seats told the house that we were not good sports in Ottawa. I should like to give some figures to show that this is not true. According to the last available figures for 1937, the value of government tax-exempt property in Ottawa was approximately $44,000,000. I understand that at the present time the value -is approximately $53,000,000, but I shall take the previous figures.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1939
speechtext:
Does that include the
parliament buildings?

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1939
speechtext:
Yes, and the hon. member should know that. He should have found that out before he spoke. This tax-exempt property is divided as follows:
Land, $8,332,375.	.
Buildings, $35,609,209.
The average tax rate is 42-5 mills. Public school supporters pay 39 mills, and separate school supporters, with many more children, pay 46 mills. This averages, as I said, 42-5 mills.
If this government were paying taxes like those our ordinary citizens have to pay, we should be receiving from the government $1,320,000 a year, whereas actually we receive only $100,000. Surely every hon. member knows, and, if not, I intend to make them aware of the fact, that eveiy time this government-and the same is true of any other federal government in the past-expropriates buildings, it is not to help the city of Ottawa, but for the purposes of improving this capital city of the dominion. Hon. gentlemen know very well that we give federal government property every protection possible.
Let me cite a few figures. From 1918 to 1937, the government took over property in the city of Ottawa assessed at $3,711,255, on. which we lost in taxes $137,692. From 1909 to 1937, expropriations by the government amounted to $5,659,555, which meant a loss in taxes to the city of $177,618. It must be remembered that these figures do not include properties owned by the federal district commission, which properties are also tax-exempt, and contribute no revenues whatsoever to the city. That is why I thought I would take time this afternoon to say a few words to inform hon. members on both sides of the house of the conditions that exist in our city.
During 1938 the government decided to expropriate practically all of Wellington street and Sparks street from Kent street, except the church. It costs so much for a church that they left that out. The properties expropriated were assessed at $920,720, and on these expropriations alone the citizens of Ottawa lost $36,000 in taxation. It has been contended that these expropriations and the con-

City oj Ottawa Agreement
struction of new government buildings increase the value of property in the city, but may I say, Mr. Speaker, that is not the case. I have lived in Ottawa for sixty years; I know what has been happening here for the last fifty years at least, and whenever there was an expropriation, as on Sussex street, for instance, business went down to nothing; stores became vacant. When the government expropriated the north side of Wellington' street the same thing happened. Every store on the south side of the street became vacant or profitable to nobody. The few who kept their buildings kept them because it was cheaper to keep them than to lease them.

speechtext: It would not enhance the beauty of the city to have stores near the parliament buildings or the new administrative buildings.

speechtext:
If my friend knew conditions in Ottawa he would not build a store on Wellington street or anywhere in Ottawa. The only buildings that have been erected on the south side of Wellington street in recent years are the United States legation; the Victoria building, owned by Edwards and company, and, of course, the Bank of Canada building. Outside these one cannot find another building that was erected following the expropriation of property. The situation was the same on Sussex street.
I am not making a plea here for myself, or making a speech for votes at all. I do not need them because my seat is safe, much safer than that of many of my hon. friends; and even if I am not here in another parliament, some other member for Ottawa will be. I am making a plea simply for what is right and for what should be done, and in my opinion Ottawa has always been too generous towards all governments, because we have had all kinds of governments in the last twenty years.
WTiat about the water service? We all know that Ottawa has probably the best water in the country. The city corporation has installed the most modern filtration plant, probably the best on this continent, at a cost of $1,500,000, and I have never heard a single complaint since then by any member that Ottawa water was not the best. It is better than one gets in Windsor. The ordinary business enterprise in Ottawa pays a flat water rate of 16-8 cents per thousand gallons, while the government enjoys a special rate of thirteen cents per thousand gallons up to two hundred million gallons, and ten cents per thousand gallons after that. The hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps), when he told the house that we were not good
sports, must not forget that our water tax is 16-5 cents, while in Winnipeg it is 38 cents.
Let me give a personal instance. I am not making a political speech at all. I am simply pleading for fairness from the government to the city of Ottawa. When I bought a property in Ottawa thirty years ago my assessment was $3,500, and the taxes amounted to $68.90. At present my taxes on that property amount to $310 a year. So am I a good sport or not? Hon. members may call me something else, if they like, and I admit I am probably foolish. With conditions as they are, it is not profitable to own property in Ottawa. Property is a white elephant.
Here is another consideration. Everybody knows that the city gives the government fire protection, police protection, and the government uses our streets, yet no government has ever given the city a five cent piece for the maintenance and repair of our streets. We have to look after all that ourselves.
Furthermore, the city purchased properties on Elgin street from Albert street to Laurier avenue four or five years ago, and for that purpose had to issue twenty-year debentures amounting to $875,000. So the government has received back many times the $100,000 that is granted to the city. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) may say that the government has spent $200,000 or more in the city of Ottawa. That is all right. They can spend what they like. That is not my lookout; that was for the beautification of the capital city. It was not for me, not for the city of Ottawa, but for everybody in Canada.
So I ask the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin), and the Minister of Finance as well, not to press the bill any further. Give us a chance. We lose every year $200,000 by the fact that through these expropriations we do not collect taxes, they are exempt every time, I believe it is only right that I should not have to pay to be a citizen of Ottawa, to be a resident of the capital city. I could go across to Hull, where I would be nearby; but I am considered to be a citizen of Ottawa, as I am, and when I speak for myself I speak for all taxpayers within the municipality. It seems to me that there is a certain lack of courage on the part of hon. members in not finding out what the country desires so far as the city of Ottawa is concerned. In 1912 a plebiscite was proposed to the citizens of Ottawa for the setting up of a federal scheme. It was voted upon and carried. At that time my hon. friends on the opposite side of the house, now the official opposition, were in power. That project never materialized; the old order has continued until to-day. If Ottawa were a federal district, nobody in this

City of Ottawa Agreement

house will deny that our taxes would be reduced. It is common sense. That is all I ask. It is useless to say any more.
I have been accused of not being in the house very often. I happen to represent a seat which keeps me elsewhere. If I were the member for Winnipeg North or the Yukon territory, I should be in this chamber all the time; I might be sleeping, sometimes, through some speeches in which I am not interested, but I would be here just the same. But it happens that I am busy outside the house, not in my own behalf but for the sake of those who are suffering. If members of the Social Credit party will listen to that they can make a good argument for themselves. I am trying to help the people, whether they are in the east or the west. I help them whenever it is possible.
After all, I repeat, why should the government not give us a fair deal? A fair deal would be to give us for ten years at least an annual grant of $200,000; and when I come here ten years from now I shall be ready to ask for more.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to lend my support to the arguments put forward by the hon. member for Ottawa East (Mr. Pinard). Since 1925 the amount of this grant has remained at $100,000; but I believe that if hon. members have listened attentively to what the hon. member for Ottawa East has had to say, they will have found convincing arguments in his statements. He has pointed to the expropriations which have been made, and which have meant a loss of revenue to the city of Ottawa. As this administration well knows, governmental costs have risen materially since 1925, and yet we are paying the city of Ottawa the same sum as we commenced to pay in that year. I think the hon. member's point is well taken. The only thing I would ask of him is not to press the suggestion that this matter be held over, but to allow it to go through, with the suggestion that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), and the government take into consideration what he has said and see whether they cannot bring forward next year a measure which will commend itself to all those who are interested in Ottawa, and particularly those who are ratepayers of this city.
We all enjoy the benefits and amenities of Ottawa. As a member, of course I find myself frequently in the position of opposing government expenditures, but I never oppose government expenditures in Ottawa for the purpose of beautification or the erection of beautiful buildings in this capital city. It is one place
IMr. Pinard. j
where they should be built. The only thing I do oppose is not getting one hundred cents on the dollar for expenditures on improvements. I believe the citizens of Ottawa, and not only they but all the citizens of Canada and those who come into our country and find an opportunity to visit the capital city, are quite satisfied with what this government and other governments have done to help make Ottawa attractive.
I did not. rise just to place a few words on Hansard. I rose without any solicitation on the part of the hon. member for Ottawa East, to give him particular support, because I felt that the arguments he put forward were sound and should be persuasive as far as this government is concerned. If there is one point for which I can commend the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), it is his desire to do his very best for Ottawa. I believe he has done so and is still doing it, and I know he has the support of every hon. member in trying to realize the ideals which he holds before himself for the capital city.
I hope the Minister of Public Works will take into account the debate this afternoon and will give consideration to the possibility of some increase in the grant to Ottawa, to be brought down at the next session of this house or the first session of the next parliament.

It is a capital city, and for purposes well known to those in charge of civic government in Ottawa it has never been intended, nor have they made any concerted effort, to make Ottawa an industrial city. The largest employers of labour in Ottawa are the government of Canada. They have practically 12,000 employees here. It should not be forgotten that Ottawa supplies the employees of the government with all those services which an up-to-date city renders to its citizens. We have in Ottawa, hospitals, schools, fire protection, police protection, water services and all the other things which in a city go to make up the public service rendered to the employees of any great organization. Mr. Chairman, the minister is mistaken when he says this bill was reported previously. What actually happened was that someone moved that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again. Had it been reported, the next step would have been the third reading.
With regard to the suggestion that I should withdraw my amendment, that would put me under a handicap, because "to-day is ours and to-morrow is not". We have before us a government bill, on which I maintain-and I think the authorities bear me out; I should like an opportunity to argue the point before a ruling is given-that it is fully competent for me to introduce an amendment such as I have suggested. If I should drop my amend-

Fisheries Act Amendment
ment and trust to the vague, distant, fortuitous possibility-for that is all it is-that a private bill, or a public bill introduced by a private member, to be strictly accurate may be reached, I may find myself in the position that my bill may never come up. Mr. Chairman, at six o'clock I was giving my reason why I preferred that my amendment should be discussed now rather than in connection with the bill of which I have given notice. Being half dead with the popular epidemic which has decimated the membership of the house, I missed giving the most succinct argument for haste in this connection. The legislature of the state of Washington is now meeting at Olympia, and in that state the vested interests which are behind the use of traps are moving heaven and earth, and some other places as well, to have repealed a law which was passed by initiative and referendum some four years ago to prohibit the use of traps in those waters. That action was not taken by legislation; it was done by what is called initiative and referendum, that is, any one can have a certain action taken by obtaining a sufficient number of votes. That action would never have been taken by the legislature. The vested interests have been laying for this legislation in order to have it repealed. They failed two years ago, but the matter is up again.
One of the greatest arguments that they advance is that the Dominion of Canada has not kept faith with the written agreement and understanding between our fishermen and theirs. They contend that they have taken out 219 traps, while we have not taken out our four or five. This is the reason for the urgency. The scope of this matter is comparatively small, but I do not know of anything that has provoked so much ill feeling in the western states and British Columbia. It has become a matter between the common people and the vested interests. During the last few weeks the feeling ran so high, according to the reports in the press, that they had to bring in the equivalent of our sergeant-at-arms to clear the galleries in the legislature. That is why I am so urgent and insistent that we should pass this amendment to-night rather than wait for six, eight or perhaps twelve weeks hence, even though the bill might pass at that time, in order to get action. If we pass it now, the argument of those who want traps restored to United States waters would be gone. The opponents of traps would be able to say that now the conditions are fair. If we do not do this, the chances are considerable that they will put back their 219 traps as against the four or five on this side.
For the sake of some of the new hon. members, I should like to explain how this thing works. The largest and most valuable run of salmon in our waters is the sockeye salmon run, the greater portion of which approaches our shores from the southwest corner of Vancouver island. Then, for some unknown reason, the fish proceed across to Puget sound, which is United States waters and where there are no spawning streams. They circle round Puget sound and many of them are taken there before they can come back into the tributaries of the Fraser river. They go up the Fraser river for a thousand or fifteen hundred miles to spawm in all the creeks and rivers. We breed the fish and the Americans capture them. Prior to the passing of this initiative legislation, they took seventy per cent of the run. The proportions could be easily calculated because the fish are coming from one place and going to one place. Since the Americans removed their 219 traps, our share of the catch has run as high as eighty-six per cent. It would pay us as sharp-dealing people, let alone for reasons of fairness and humanity, to pension off the forty-one employees who are engaged to operate these traps, although I think the number is less than that, in order to retain
Fisheries Act Amendment

such a high proportion of the salmon. This is quite apart from the extra employment that would be given if these traps were removed.
I should like to explain just how a trap works. I have a sketch of one which I exhibit. The fish come round a headland and make for the Fraser river. The instinct of the homing salmon is just as great as that of the homing pigeon, and they cannot go anywhere else but around that headland. They go along the shore-line and they come up to a lead, as it is called, which may be 600 feet or 6,000 feet long. It is stretched out to a trap. They cannot get through there and they cannot get out on the shore, so they nose along until they come to the mouth of the trap. There are wings on each side of the mouth. They go through the mouth, and finally they reach a place with a little hole like the neck of those ink-bottles which you cannot upset. Once in there, they cannot turn round. They are then brailed out.
The law is that for forty-eight hours in the week this mouth or gate here must be closed. The gate may be closed; but as the fish come along on Friday and Saturday nights and find they cannot get through, they simply mill round and round. You or I would go down round one side or the other and get past the trap, but that is not fish nature. They simply mill round, and their instinct guides them until they start up again, when they again hit this lead. Then they mill round again. On Monday morning there are just three times as many fish as there were on Friday morning. Ninety per cent of the fish stay there. That is what the wing is intended for.
Then what is the net? The net has what is called a two-inch extension. It is two inches when it is extended. Consequently, the square of the mesh is exactly one inch each way, and that is the measure of the fish that can get through there. Anything which is less than an inch can get through. Last year or the year before we kept track of it. They caught everything-whales, barracuda, rat fish, porpoises-all down the line. I think they stopped at shrimps. We did not get any shrimps, but we got everything else. Nothing escaped them-mature, immature, day and night, in season and out of season. It is an enormously destructive method of fishing, and the whole idea that one man or two men should be allowed such a particular privilege is against all sense of common decency and what we call public policy. The people who advocate a thing like that are in line with the people who, if not to-day, not so long ago thought that the whole of Canada west of the great lakes-

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932   ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OP OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OP FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: It is about forty years since they started that. It is about time it was changed.

They have had forty years of it and have made fortunes out of it. As I was saying, people who advocate a thing like that are like the people who advocated that all Canada west of the great lakes belonged to the Hudson Bay company, or that India belonged to the East India Company because at one time it had huge territorial rights. But we are living in the present age, not in the past.
To cut a long story short, I shall try to meet the minister half way. This is a matter which will be settled only when it is settled aright. It will ring down through Canada's political record for a long time to come until it is settled. It is now becoming a provincial matter, though there is no need in the world for that; before we know where we are, it will become a national matter.
During the dinner recess I considered my position carefully, and in the interests of those whom I ostensibly represent I am going to take a great chance, which I am not authorized to take, on behalf of them, and make this proposal, which would almost impel, I hope and think, acceptance by the minister. The one I propose to insert is this. I might as well say, just to contrast the two, that the previous amendment was that:
No one shall use a salmon trap net in any of the Pacific waters of Canada.
That is withdrawn. The amendment I now
propose is:
After the calendar year 1939 no one shall use a salmon trap net in any of the Pacific waters of Canada off the southwesterly shores of Vancouver island.
That will have the great advantage, if it passes to-night, that it will be telegraphed to Olympia and it will save the situation

Fisheries Act Amendment
there. That is the all important thing. The general principle, too, is urgent, on account of the work it will make for individuals- seiners, trailers, gill netters.
The cannery men with the exception of one, are in favour of the elimination of these licences. This is giving them another year of life, and one year of a privilege of that kind is valuable. It has been suggested that there is vested capital involved which should not be rudely dispossessed, but the whole fishery law is based upon the fact that you get a licence for one season only, and you are liable to lose it: even in the middle of the season you can lose it if the Department of Fisheries says, "We are not going to allow any more fishing in that area." You may have a cannery there, but you are out of luck; that is all. And it is all done in the interests of conservation.
The same thing applies here. No injustice will be done to these people. They knew their licence was an annual one. The traps are taken out every year. They are not yet put in for this year, and how is the time to tell these people they will not be given a licence this year. This is 1939. They cannot say they have not been given notice or warning, because in 1936 they were told in writing-I have it here-that their licences would not be renewed after 1936. This is 1939, and they are still being renewed. Can any great injustice be done to people who have had that amount of warning? I do not think so. So they will have had ample warning if they get a licence this year as well. They are being treated with more than leniency; they are being treated with favour. After they have had this privilege for some thirty or forty years and have made several fortunes out of it, I think they might well give way in the interests of conservation, in the interests of allowing employment to our fishermen, and above all in the interests of encouraging the Americans to keep their traps out-which means so very much to us.
At this stage I propose to stop, and hopefully suggest to the minister that he might accept that position. I have some other data on the subject; but it will be needless to give it if the minister can see his way, and I earnestly hope that he may do so. If it were necessary I would go down on my knees in sackcloth and ashes, humbling myself to the minister to urge him to undo this great injustice, not of his doing, but of his perpetuating. I know that the people of British Columbia, with very few exceptions, and those entirely of people who have got a very gilt-edged axe to grind, would be in favour of the course I suggest. I pause here to ask the
minister if he can see his way to accept this very much modified amendment which I have proposed.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932   ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OP OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OP FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext:
The first point I want
to raise is that this amendment anticipates a matter which is already before the house by way of a bill introduced by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), Bill No, 30 on the order paper. The hon. member suggests that section 12 of the Fisheries Act be amended by the insertion of the following:
12A. Notwithstanding anything to the contrary in this act or regulations thereunder, no person shall use, for the taking of salmon, any salmon trap net in any Canadian tidal waters of the coast of British Columbia.
Although the wording of the amendment now suggested differs slightly from the provisions of the bill which is on the order paper, the principle is the same, and I submit that, under standing order 31, paragraph (d) of section 6, no motion shall anticipate a matter which has been previously appointed for consideration by the house, or with reference to which a notice of motion has been previously given and not withdrawn.
Second, this is citation 398, under standing order 48:
An amendment cannot anticipate a notice of motion on the order paper.
It is all the same principle, Mr. Chairman, namely, that a matter cannot be brought up by amendment anticipating any other matter which is already down on the order paper and which may come before the house for discussion during the session. On this ground I feel that it would be out of order to accept the amendment or to discuss the matter at this stage.
Further, the amendment, I submit, is contrary to the rules and to standing order 76 because it seeks to add to a bill before the house a matter which is not dealt with by the bill. Bill No. 15 which is now under consideration is to amend section 57 of the
Fisheries Act Amendment

Fisheries Act. The proposed amendment seeks to add a new provision to the Fisheries Act, and to change altogether a section of the Fisheries Act that has not been brought before the house. Citation 781, under standing order 76, provides, with reference to amendments in committee:
An amendment must be relevant both to the subject matter of the bill. . . .
The amendment is not relevant to the subject matter of the bill because the subject matter of the bill is to amend section 57 of the Fisheries Act. Further, to quote from the same citation 781:
It must not be based on schedules or other provisions the terms of which have not been placed before the committee; it must not be beyond the scope of the bill.
The scope of the bill under consideration is the amending of section 57 of the Fisheries Act, and the proposed amendment seeks to amend section 12 of the Fisheries Act. It is, therefore, altogether beyond the scope of the bill now before us, and I submit that we are violating the rules of the house in proceeding in this manner.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932   ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OP OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OP FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon.
minister has raised two separate points of order. I think it would have been better if we had confined ourselves to one at a time, but possibly he is going on the well known doctrine that two weak arguments are better than one sound one, because taken separately there is absolutely nothing in them. But there is strength in union, just as it is more difficult to break a bundle of sticks tied together than to break the sticks singly, one by one.
As to the first point of order he raised, that I was anticipating a matter which has already been set down for the consideration of the house, he lightly passed over the obvious fact that the two matters are not related to each other except in a stepfatherly manner. I may be cautious and that is why to some extent I changed the amendment to this bill in order that it could not possibly be open to the objection which the minister raises. The original proposal was as the minister read it, to forbid once and for all, and forever more, all salmon fishing traps in the Pacific waters of Canada.
