speechtext: Of British Columbia.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932   ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OP OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OP FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext:
The waters of the Pacific coast of Canada I think was the wording, but it does not make any difference. This is allcomprehensive, all-including, so to speak, and beginning from the moment this bill becomes law. But the amendment which I have now proposed, and which I do not think the min-

ister could have thoroughly studied is wholly different; for it says, "After the calendar year 1939." That is a whale of a difference. If some one is getting thirty or forty thousand dollars a year from a privilege, it makes a big difference to him whether he is to be cut off now or a year from now.
The second point of disresemblance, so to speak, is that the original amendment said: in all the Pacific waters of Canada-or it may have been British Columbia. The amendment I have proposed to-night is limited to a strictly small area off the southwest coast of Vancouver island, a distance of probably eleven to fifteen miles; I think it is eleven miles, as a matter of fact. There is surely a big difference there, Mr. Chairman.
As regards the second point of order which the minister dealt with, I was going to say that it was even more inappropriate, but there can be no degrees; for if a thing is out of order it is out of order. He said that my present amendment is not in order because he has introduced a bill to amend section 57 of the Fisheries Act, and therefore, if I move an amendment to his bill it must be relevant to and in some way connected with the subject matter of section 57. That is fine and dandy, if it were so, but it is not so. He did not introduce a bill to amend section 57 of the Fisheries Act at all. I ask you to look at it, Mr. Chairman. It is "An act to amend the Fisheries Act "-that, and that only.
I have right before my eyes an illustration that I have just picked up. The hon. member for Jacques-Cartier (Mr. Matlette) introduced Bill No. 10, to amend the criminal code (sweepstakes). In other words, the criminal code is an act that applies to a great many things; to particularize and narrow his amendment down to the matter of sweepstakes his bill is entitled, "An act to amend the criminal code (sweepstakes)," and under that bill I could not bring in any amendment that was not connected with sweepstakes. Had he merely said, " an act to amend the criminal code," I or any other member could have brought in an amendment to do away with capital punishment, had it so pleased us. The distinction is clear, and what the minister has quoted refers to a case like that. He says that the amendment is beyond the scope of the bill-"scope and title of the bill," those words which are found in the section he did not quote. Now the scope of the bill is to amend the Fisheries Act, that and that only. It is not my fault or his that he did not particularize it in the way the criminal code amendment bill did with reference to sweepstakes. The fact remains that he did not, and it is therefore the privilege of any member to

Fisheries Act Amendment
amend the act, provided he keeps within the scope and title of the bill which is to amend the Fisheries Act.
Let me quote from Bourinot. Some hon. members quote from May; but I prefer Bourinot as a Canadian authority, and at one time clerk of this house. The English authorities are not so familiar with our customs. Bourinot says:
The committee of the whole have now power to make amendments not within the scope and title of the bill.
The power goes further than I do. It covers even cases where the amendment is not within the scope of the bill:
But if any amendment be not within the title of the bill, the committee are to amend the title accordingly.
They can even do that if it is necessary, and there was a case in point. At page 534 of Bourinot this rule is laid down:
It is irregular to propose an amendment which is irrelevant to the subject-matter of a clause.
If I stopped there, as the minister did, it would be said I am introducing an amendment which is irrelevant to the subject-matter of the clause. But listen to the rest of the sentence-because one cannot take one's law piecemeal, reading half a sentence and leaving out the other half:
-but it-
That is the amendment.

should be submitted to the committee at the end of the bill, as a separate clause.
That indicates clearly it is contemplated that such action might be and can be taken. We have precedents, and lawyers love precedents. Let us look at them. Here is Bourinot again:
The house went into committee on a bill "to amend the general acts respecting railways"-
Just like the general title of such enactments as the act to amend the Fisheries Act.
-and a question arose whether it was competent to add a clause requiring the government to purchase goods for the use of dominion railways upon public tender and contract only; and the committee having arisen for the purpose of receiving instructions from the house upon the point at issue, Mr. Speaker Anglin-
A celebrated speaker.

decided that such an amendment would be regular without an instruction.
That is, a definite instruction. There is no question that it is held to be legal to amend a bill within the scope and title of the bill. The only condition imposed is that if you go outside the title of the bill you must amend the title as well. That is not
what I proposed to do. I hold that the point of order is entirely wrong. I have already quoted Bourinot. Further on he states:
A committee of the whole have now power-
Many years ago the situation was different, but we are living to-day not before confederation.
-to make amendments not within the scope and title of the bill.
But the amendment proposed was within the scope and title of the bill. I need not argue that point because obviously the amendment is within the scope and title of the bill. If it were not, my case would be gone. Now he is trying to build up an argument on something he wishes he had done but did not do. I submit that on both points the objection is out of order.

speechtext:
Anyone who is familiar with conditions on the Pacific coast will recognize the merit of the argument advanced by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. There is a distinct difference between the terms of his amendment and the terms of the bill that now stands in his name for second reading. I say, there is an essential difference, and in that respect it cannot be held that the amendment which the hon. gentleman has just read and which is now before the committee anticipates in any respect the bill that stands on the order paper. Furthermore, I refer to citation 769 under standing order 76, page 221 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms:
It shall be an instruction to all committees of the whole house to which bills may be committed that they have power to make such amendments therein as they shall think fit; provided they be relevant to the subject matter of the bill; but that if any such amendments shall not be within the title of the bill they do amend the title accordingly and do report the same specially to the house.
The adoption of the amendment moved by the hon. member would not necessitate a change in the title of the bill, "An Act to Amend the Fisheries Act," and it is therefore properly within the jurisdiction of the committee to consider the amendment.
May I go a step beyond that and appeal to the minister not to press his point of order at this stage. This matter is of great public interest at the coast, and any attempt to block discussion at this time by invoking any rule of order might be misconstrued there as an effort to obscure public discussion of a question which is of such vital consequence to the fishing industry of British Columbia.

speechtext:
The Minister of Fisheries referred to Bill No. 30 now on the order paper, sponsored by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). I read from that bill:
The Fisheries Act, 1932, chapter 42 of the statutes of 1932. is amended by adding thereto, immediately after section 12, the following section:
"12A. Notwithstanding anything to the contrary in this act or regulations thereunder, no

person shall use, for the taking of salmon, any salmon trap net in any Canadian tidal waters of the coast of British Columbia."
The amendment moved by the hon. member to-night reads:
That the following be inserted as a new section:
"Section 32 is hereby amended by inserting the following as subsection 2 thereof:
After the calendar year 1939 no one shall use a salmon trap net in any of the Pacific waters of Canada off the southwesterly shores of Vancouver island.
I quote from Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, page 225, citation 792:

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932   ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OP OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OP FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext:
I regret very much that the minister took the point of order which he did, thereby suggesting that he would in that way evade the responsibility of meeting the situation, and the more so because it will be within the recollection of the committee that a few weeks ago when this question of the action in the legislature at Olympia first came up, I brought it up on the orders of the day, asking whether he was prepared to take the responsibility of continuing the traps on this side; and he said on that occasion-I will not take the trouble to read it-that the matter of reciprocity, that is keeping out our traps as long as they, kept theirs out, was still under consideration. I could think of no more appropriate moment than the present to make an announcement of his policy. Not only has he not seen his way to give a favourable decision, but he apparently lacks the intention to make that decision at all. Now time goes on. The minister has apparently not yet made up his mind. I wonder when he is going to have it made up, because the prepara-

Fisheries Act Amendment
tions for building the traps have already begun. We are told here that the matter is being considered, but work is already going on in preparation for putting in these traps. Are they doing that with some whisper in their ears, "Go ahead, it will be all right"? I have a letter under my hand dated February 22, which reads:
Perhaps you do not know that they have started the usual procedure a week ago putting piles in the water off the spit where they keep them in the winter. I live here 250 yards from where they are working and it seems that they are sure of putting the traps in. I understand they are putting in five traps this year.
So now it comes down to the one brief moment that the advocates of freedom in this matter can have to discuss the merits of this question. I have put it before the committee at some length already, but I am going to clinch it by an indisputable and most reliable authority. I hold in my hand six letters, five of them signed by the deputy minister of fisheries and one by the minister himself. I may have put the case badly, ignorantly, incompletely, and laoking the eloquence which it requires, but I will take the written word of the minister himself as to whether or not these traps should be taken out. I will read only one letter, the one addressed to myself, but there were five others to different fishery associations and others. The one addressed to myself is dated February 7, 1936, three years and almost one month ago. It reads: Dear Mr. Neill:	.
I wish to revert to your letter of June 25 last-
That is 1935, when this matter was brought in its immediate form to his attention.

endorsing a petition by the Kyuoquot Trollers' Cooperative Association, urging that licence for salmon trap-nets in the portion of the southwest coast of Vancouver island be discontinued.
The question has been receiving careful consideration and, in the light of all the circumstances, it has been decided to continue such licences, for 1936. Notification is being given the licensees, however, that thereafter such licences will not be granted. If trap nets are reintroduced in the state of Washington-
Which is what I have been talking about.

the question of reallowing them in the above area will again be considered.
That is signed by the deputy minister, and the minister now assumes the responsibility. Substantially the same letter, except that the name was different, was addressed to W. R Gray, secretary of the British Columbia Fishermen's Protective Association, New Westminster, and the Fishing Vessels Owners' Association of British Columbia, Vancouver, and a letter to the chief supervisor of fisheries, giving him orders to carry it out.
The last letter, from which I want to quote briefly, was addressed by the minister to J. II. Todd & Son, one of the owners of these traps. Evidently Mr. Todd had telegraphed a protest when this notice was served on him by the chief supervisor. I shall not quote the earlier part of the letter unless the _ minister asks for it, but this is the pertinent part:
Your company may rest assured that the above decision-
That is the unfavourable decision against them.
-was reached only after carefully weighing all factors in connection with the matter.
The important part is, the minister states that he felt it was necessary to take the steps he had taken, but this is the postscript:
There is the further very strong argument, that the continuance of traps on our side will operate as an incentive for rescinding the prohibition of traps in Washington state.
Is that not what I have been preaching here? That is his own opinion. The minister says that:
In the light of these conditions, the urge was very strong that trap licences should be renewed by my department for the present year-
That was 1936.
-but in view of the investment in these traps and the preparations already made for their operation for the coming season, it was finally decided that in the public interest-
"In the. public interest."
[DOT]-the traps should not be discontinued then but should be allowed for the present year so that fair notice should be given to the owners and operators thereof; and it was stipulated that should traps be reintroduced on the United States side their prohibition in the Sooke area would be reconsidered.
That is no ex parte statement by me; that is the statement of the minister himself. He says that his department have carefully considered it, and that was their serious and considered decision, but as a concession to the vested interests they would be allowed to continue for 1936 but the licences should not be renewed thereafter.
We had this matter up before a committee of the house, and I remember very well one member of the committee said, "Mr. Minister, you changed your policy, you refused to issue these licences beyond 1936. and you have now changed your mind or your policy or both; will you explain the reason for this change of mind." But we have not heard that reason yet, and I hope we may get it to-night. It will need to be a pretty sound and substantial reason to combat the decision, carefully arrived at, as the minister himself says, after full consideration and in the light of all the circumstances, backed up by his officials, that these traps must not be per-
Fisheries Act Amendment

mitted after 1936, that they would be allowed until that year as a concession to the vested interests. In that committee I made the same suggestion that I made to-night, that they should be permitted to continue for 1937 as well, in order that there might be no possible chance for the vested interests-always so dear to the heart of any government-to say they had not been fairly dealt with. Now we have the attitude the minister has exhibited to-night, that he is not going to accept any suggestion or compromise at all, that the traps are going to continue and will continue, I suppose, as long as he has control of them.
I can tell the minister that this is a very unpopular move in British Columbia. It is not a question of thirty, forty, fifty or two hundred fishermen; it has become an issue between the common people and the vested interests-and in this case the vested interests are very small. It is not a question even between the fishermen and the cannerymen, who themselves are against these traps, with the exception of this one man. One hon. member of the house rose in the committee and said: "Gentlemen, I am getting a -little tired of this. As most of you know, I am a canneryman, and if I could have a trap at my door, as this man has, I could get all the fish I needed with fifteen or twenty men. But I am quite willing to do without a trap and use between two and four hundred men in order to preserve the fish, in order not to have them taken out at all stages of their development, and in order to make work for the fishermen." But he very properly added, "I cannot see why, if thirty-six canneries can get along without traps, the thirty-seventh cannery cannot do the same thing."
' There is the issue. It is not the fishermen versus the canneries; it is the common people versus one gigantic, firmly entrenched, allembracing monopoly. The people of British Columbia will call their members and the government of the day to account when this question comes before them in the next election.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932   ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OP OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OP FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext:
I should like to support the remarks of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. My experience since this matter was last discussed in the house has strengthened my conviction that traps should be abolished. These traps always were a menace to the fishing industry in British Columbia and, by reason of the situation that has developed in the state of Washington, they are a still greater menace to-day. I believe it is in the public interest that no further licences be issued for the operation of stationary fish traps.

It is not to-day so much an issue of threatened unemployment in the fishing industry or violation of the principles of conservation. The issue is that the policies pursued by the minister will result in turning over to United States operators the business that properly belongs to Canadian operators. The fishing industry along the coast of British Columbia is important to those of us who reside in that province. The minister is well aware, as are other members of the house, that certain legislation is now pending in the state of Washington, sponsored by Senator Edwards who has openly stated time and again that it is his purpose to restore the fish traps in United States waters immediately south of Point Roberts and the international boundary. He intends, he says, to rehabilitate the ghost town of Blaine, Washington.
It is well known that, prior to 1935, United States operators had something like 219 traps, and that by reason of the fact that they operated traps in those waters they obtained an average of between sixty and seventy per cent of the Fraser river sockeye salmon pack. For reasons of conservation, and because there was a gentleman's agreement in this respect between the Canadian and United States authorities, the state of Washington abolished their traps by legislation which became effective in 1935. What was the result? The average Canadian share of the Fraser river sockeye salmon pack prior to 1935 was about thirty per cent. In 1936 our average rose to fifty-three per cent; in 1937 it was about eighty per cent, and I am reliably informed that last season it was over sixty per cent. Surely that is an important point. The chief reason for the agitation in the state of Washington in favour of the proposed legislation is that the Canadian government has continued to permit the operation of stationary fish traps at Sooke, in disregard of the gentleman's agreement and, may I say, in disregard of well established principles of conservation.
I do not wish to traverse all the ground covered by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. but the house should fully understand the position in which the government finds itself in regard to this issue. These traps have been operating under licence since 1918 at the southwesterly tip of Vancouver island, where they may intercept the main migration of the sockeye before they pass through United States waters to the mouth of the Fraser river. It is an extraordinary monopoly; these people are permitted to operate under conditions that are denied thousands of

Fisheries Act Amendment
commercial fishermen who stake their livelihood on the operation of their vessels and gear in the coastal waters of British Columbia. These traps, as the reports of the department indicate, catch everything from herrings to whales while they are fishing, and usually they fish from April to November. They catch sockeye before the ordinary gill netter can put out and catch sockeye. They catch immature fish. It is true they say that they donate the immature fish to the hospitals of Vancouver; but surely that is no justification, and certainly it does not cover up their crimes in that regard. When I think of all the restrictive regulations imposed upon the ordinary commercial gill netter, purse seiner and troller in the waters of British Columbia, I think I have a right to feel indignant at the extraordinary privileges enjoyed by the operation of the Sooke traps. The ordinary fisherman is penalized if he attempts to moor his gear to shore or to the bottom. He is prohibited from operating a drifting trap-net. He is compelled to observe certain stipulated closed seasons. It is true that the regulations in regard to closed seasons apply to the Sooke operators as well, but it is a well known fact that on account of the type of construction of the traps which, as the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has explained, extend two or three thousand feet out to sea, the fish are held under favourable tidal conditions, waiting until the apron of the trap is lifted at the expiration of the closed season.
There is a marked contrast between the conditions under which the ordinary commercial gill netter, purse seiner and troller operate and the privileges extended to the Sooke operators. At Sooke they employ something like forty-one men; they can winch up large quantities of fish in nets of dose mesh into waiting barges for convenient transport to the Empire cannery at Esquimalt. According to the evidence given before the committee, that was the number of men employed; but it was never clearly or satisfactorily explained why they could not put that many or more men in employment if they were willing to adopt the same type of vessels as those used by the United States operators who fish further out in that area.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni has made it clear that the minister promised the organized fishermen of British Columbia that he would discontinue the issuance of these licences in the public interest, and the fishermen have been at a complete loss to understand why the minister has not fulfilled his promise. I have taken pains to meet the organized fishermen. I think all the organizations on the coast, with two exceptions, discussed this matter this season when they met in convention, and they say this amounts to nothing but a double-cross on the part of the dominion government. They say, "We have been double-crossed. We were promised that the traps would be wiped out, but they are still being operated, and we have evidence that it is intended to continue them in operation for the season of 1939." We all know very well what happened. After the minister gave his promise, some officials of the British Columbia government, the operators in question and their financial backers organized a high pressure, costly lobby, to which we were exposed in the Canadian House of Commons.
The minister indicated clearly to the committee which sat on this matter that it was his intention, no matter what the report of the committee might be, to issue licences. No one can understand clearly the minister's attitude in this matter, unless he is determined to protect the profits of the privileged interests at Sooke and disregard completely the interests of the large fishing industry of British Columbia. It is now clearer than ever before that the fishing industry of British Columbia is menaced by the continued operation of the traps at Sooke.
I cannot be too emphatic with regard to the traps. They violate the regulations under the act, as was shown in evidence; they violate the principles of conservation, particularly with regard to catching immature fish and the mutilation of fish which are held when milling round within the spiller and the heart of the trap. Piracy is sometimes described as an act of depredation on the high seas, but these traps are committing acts of depredation on the fishing industry just as much as if they were boarding Canadian fishing vessels and looting them. It is piracy on the high seas. I think at this time the minister should make clear his intention to discontinue the issuance of licences for the stationary traps at Sooke.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to join
the other two hon. members in protesting against the use of traps on the southerly point of Vancouver island. Most of the points with regard to this matter have been covered, but there are one or two matters I should like to draw to the attention of the minister and the committee. It is true that the Americans use traps in some of their fishing grounds, but they are up in the north. In the great areas on Bristol bay where the salmon run, no salmon traps or power boats are allowed, so great is the care taken by the Americans to preserve the salmon run. We should take similar care in connection with
Fisheries Act Amendment

the salmon fisheries of the Fraser river. The last speaker referred to the traps catching anything from herring to whale. I have before me a list of the varieties of fish caught in the traps, and I know it will surprise some hon. members to be told that some twenty-two varieties of fish are caught. However, the most striking thing is the catch of sockeye salmon which is taken early in the month of May and the beginning of June, before the sockeye fishing really commences on the Fraser river.
For a moment I can speak as a member of the international Pacific salmon fisheries commission, which is doing everything possible to rehabilitate the great salmon runs on the Fraser river. The one variety which we are endeavouring to rehabilitate is the early run of the sockeye. Immediately upon leaving the strait this run heads for the waters of the Fraser, but the fish are caught long before the fishermen on the Fraser river have commenced fishing operations. The traps do catch immature fish and in that way are destructive. Every fishermen's organization that I know of, with the exception of perhaps one in Victoria and Nanaimo, are in favour of the elimination of traps.
Last fall I took occasion to go down to Bellingham with a view to finding out what the United States fishermen thought of the Canadian traps. I found the opinion of the United States fishermen was similar to that expressed by the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill) and the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil). They felt that the retention of traps in Canadian waters was being used by the United States interests as an argument to again have traps in the United States waters. That fight is going on at the present time. I say in all seriousness that if traps are again brought into use in United States waters they can point to the traps in Canadian waters as something that helped to bring that about.
I do not intend to traverse the ground which was covered last year and again to-night. I rise in - my place to join with other hon. members in protesting as strongly as I can against the operation of fish traps at Sooke. I thought we would have had a better chance to discuss traps when the bill introduced by the hon. member for Comox-AIberni was before the house for discussion, but as the matter has come up to-night I feel it incumbent to place myself on record as being entirely opposed to the operation of traps at Sooke. I ask the minister to reconsider the amendment offered by the hon. member, which at least contains a loop-hole for the minister, in that

it asks that they remain this year, but that notice be given that no traps will be allowed next year in the strait of Juan de Fuca.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to remind the minister and the members of the committee that this somewhat vexed subject was considered some two years ago by the standing committee on marine and fisheries. The resolution which was referred to that committee reads:
That the question of the advisability of the government issuing trap fishing licences in British Columbia waters be referred to the standing committee on marine and fisheries for study and report.
In other words, that the committee deal with the whole question of whether or not there should be traps, not only in the Sooke area but anywhere on the Pacific coast. The committee held fourteen sittings and heard several witnesses including representatives of the Department of Fisheries, the trap owners and the fishermen. I quote from the report:
In considering this question the committee has had in view the great importance of the salmon fishing industry in British Columbia waters, and the necessity for the conservation of the fish supply, the preservation of the quality of the pack and the furnishing of the greatest measure of employment.
Further, being satisfied of the great need for conservation of the fish and the avoiding of all wanton and useless destruction of this great food resource, your committee recommends that the Department of Fisheries continue to work in cooperation with the authorities in the United States with such object in view.
Right here let me say that I think the Department of Fisheries should know exactly what is being done in the state of Washington If they have not kept in touch with the situation they should be censured. They should find out at once what the position is. The committee then went on to say:
We also submit the following recommendations :
1.	That no more trap licences be granted in British Columbia waters except in the so-called Sooke area, and concerning which we are unable to come to a decision as to whether they should be continued or not, without the opportunity of securing further information.
I think the minister will agree that in principle the committee were against fish traps. They felt that there should be no fish traps on the Pacific coast and there was strong feeling against them in the Sooke area. The committee then went on to recommend:
2.	That, if the said traps are allowed in the so-called Sooke area, the licence fee for each trap be $500 per annum for each trap licence, commencing with the year 1937.
3.	That an opening of suitable size be made in the lead of such traps in order that the fish may have a better opportunity of passing on towards the spawning grounds when the trap is closed.

Fisheries Act Amendment
4.	That the department should be careful to see that the regulations providing for the closing of traps in use, for forty-eight hours per week, be rigidly enforced, and that the traps be subject to the same regulations as regards opening and closing seasons as prescribed for all varieties of fishing under the Fisheries Act and regulations.
5.	That all inspectors or guardians employed by the Department of Fisheries be independent of all fishing companies or fishing plant owners.
6.	That for the next year or two the check made in connection with the catch, as well as the escapement of sockeye and other varieties of salmon in the Sooke area be made with great care and detail so that the records expressed in both cases and numbers may be as accurate as possible.
That was the unanimous finding of the committee. Two years have passed, and I suggest that at the present time the government should know just what is the position in that area.
Personally I think the traps should be abolished. I do suggest to the minister that the question should not be left in the air. The government have the power by regulation to prevent the use of traps to-morrow, and I submit that the problem should not be allowed to drift along any further. Apparently there has been nothing done in the last two years. If anything has been done, the minister should explain to the committee to-night just what steps have been taken. If the government will not act now to stop this fishing by traps, I suggest that they at least send this bill to the marine and fisheries committee this year for consideration in detail.
' Mr. PELLETIER: Mr. Chairman, I desire to associate myself with the hon. members who have already spoken on this question. I was a member of the committee which considered this matter, and I feel it is necessary that our stand should be made quite clear. Although we may not know very much about the technical details of fishing traps, there is a principle involved that should not be ignored. It is quite clear that licensing to operate these fishing traps must to a certain degree discriminate against the fishermen of British Columbia. Although we are not so much concerned with the technical details of these traps, we do insist as a matter of principle that the government should live up to the policy laid down by the minister in 1936, and I join with other members in urging the minister to state clearly and definitely why he has found it necessary to change the attitude he took in 1936. As a member of the committee I desire to take this opportunity to make it plain that I am in entire support of the attitude taken by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) and other hon.
members who have spoken, because there is a principle involved, the protection of the fishermen of British Columbia.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, since the introduction of this bill into the house I have been tempted many times to rise in my' place on a question of privilege to draw attention to an outbreak of a peculiar disease in British Columbia. One form of this disease it is quite true is endemic everywhere among fishermen, wherever one type of fisherman finds himself in competition with another type. The gill netter gets a fever the moment he experiences contact and competition with the purse seiner, and both of them are very much disturbed when they have to come into competition with a trawler.
But this particular disease which is rampant in British Columbia is epidemic; every type of fisherman appears to be in a state of fever against one particular type, and it is that to which I want to draw attention.
Fishermen, their whole families and friends, will join together and become afflicted with this disease, infected from one to the other. The strange thing about this peculiar disease is that it creates high fever, foaming at the mouth, and an absurd desire to run around signing petitions whenever the word "Sooke" or "fish-traps" is used. As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that this disease should be called "fishtrapitis." Though it is not a very infectious disease, it does have allergic reactions, and I have noticed in British Columbia that a group of woodworkers in the centre of Vancouver island who know nothing about fishing except that a few of their number take to fishing during the season -this group of woodworkers, affiliated with the International Woodworkers of the World, a communist guided Committee of Industrial Organization, have suddenly caught the fever and babbled against the hon. member for Nanaimo in a way in which they would not have attempted to do had they realized his attitude towards organized labour.
The whole trouble is that people not connected with the fishing industry have also become suspect. The people in the interior of British Columbia find themselves suddenly seized with fever the moment they hear the word " trap." To many people " trap " has a sinister sound. They cannot recognize the similarity between the word " trap " and the word " net." It has a sinister connotation in their minds, and they are consequently apt to become infected with this peculiar disease. As a matter of fact, they pity the poor fish and try to put themselves in its place, and by considering the tragic death of these fish in
Fisheries Act Amendment

the Sooke fish traps they lament that the fish should come to the dinner table from that direction.
The whole thing is something that has to [DOT]be taken very lightly. The light of truth must be brought into this whole matter, and the breezy air of a common sense understanding of the situation must solve this question and bring relief to this terrible fever. But we have had this thing so often, one time after another, that I want to refer to a petition that was introduced into the house at this time last session.
As reported at page 683 of Hansard for last year the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) presented a petition signed by one man and 9,594 other persons. If every item in this petition were true, we should have to take serious account of it; but I submit, Mr. Chairman, that many statements in this petition are exaggerated just sufficiently to make an emotional and effusive appeal, and I said so at the time.
The petition begins in poetic fashion:
Since time immemorial large runs of soekeye salmon have passed the southwest coast of Vancouver island thence passing into American waters in Puget sound and then back to Canadian waters to spawn in the Fraser river.
From time immemorial! These people know exactly that since beyond living memory these fish have been doing this thing. As a matter of fact, the Fraser river is a comparatively young river, geologically speaking, and we do not yet know how the spawning of fish in the Fraser river acquired the peculiar conditions attaching to it which we know to-day. The petition goes on:
That for many years we have maintained in the neighbourhood of Sooke on the southwest coast of Vancouver island four or five fish traps and the Americans maintained in their waters in Puget sound several hundreds-
That is not correct.
-with the result that our percentage of the joint catch of that run would run about 30 per cent, while theirs would be 70 per cent.
That, three years ago, the Americans took out all their traps in Puget Sound numbering 219, while we retained ours, with the result that our proportion of the joint catch jumped from 30 to 50 per cent and even 80 per cent.
I want to challenge those statements definitely. Much of the material which I have obtained for the refutation of these claims of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) and his other friends are found in official records, the Department of Fisheries report 1937-38, and bulletins of the Department of Fisheries, Washington, Nos. 37 and 38.
The moment this matter was brought up in the house I referred it to Mr. Charles F. Goodrich, president of the Sooke Harbour Fishing and Packing Company, Limited, and I told him that if he had any matter to bring before me he should do so immediately. I did not do this to bolster up a monopoly. I did it to acquaint a gentleman conducting a legal business in British Columbia with the conditions that were obtaining in this house as concerned his business. Therefore, if I make quotations from the letters that he has sent me, I trust it will be understood that I personally believe every statement to be correct, and in any event they are open to the judgment of hon. members. He states:
As to Puget sound having sacrificed 219 pound nets, it should be understood that this number represents the number of licences issued, not the number of trap nets or pound nets actually in operation. Under the state of Washington regulations, it was only necessary to construct a trap net once in every four years. Consequently there were always many more licences issued than trap nets operated. In 1934, the last year traps operated there, there were some 215 licences issued and about 75 traps actually operated.
For the sake of accuracy, therefore, we should use the number 75 instead of 219.
Were the statements included in Mr. Neill's question correct, can anything be more absurd than to suppose that the continuation or the discontinuance of the five traps at Sooke would be any material factor in deciding the question in the state of Washington of whether they do or do not amend their Initiative No. 77?
Now, then, as to the question of thirty per cent having crept up to fifty and even eighty per cent, as has been repeatedly stated by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, let me quote from official sources showing the pack of Fraser river sockeyes caught in Fraser river, Sooke trap nets, and Puget Sound for the years 1935, 1936, 1937 and 1938:

I should be
glad to listen to the hon. member when I have finished. That fact-finding commission is at present gathering facts for the purpose of making recommendations in connection with the rehabilitation of the salmon industry on the Pacific coast, and any interference with their activities can only prejudice the case beforehand. I want to assure hon. members that very free use was made last year of the Sooke traps in tagging live salmon and setting them free in order that the commission might discover where these fish ultimately found their way.
But we come back to the petition:
The fact that we have not taken out our traps has been used and will be used as a very strong argument by the American trap owners for permission to reintroduce traps on the American side.
Let me counter that by reading a statement from Mr. Goodrich under date February 21, as follows:.
We have tried to keep in touch with this situation and so far as we can learn the decision does not hinge in the slightest degree upon whether the five trap nets at Sooke are continued or not. Up to the present time they have scarcely been mentioned. It is possible, of course, that they will be mentioned, and that it will also be mentioned that the United 71492-95
States federal congress after thorough investigation decided that there was no good ground for discontinuing the trap nets in Alaska.
The outcome, however, does not hinge upon the action of either the Canadian fishery department or the United States congress. The governor of the state of Washington and the state supervisor of fisheries both favour the restoration of trap net fishing, at least so far as the area in which sockeyes and pinks form the principal part of the catch. The only thing which may deter them is the attitude of the purse seiners, who are seeking to monopolize the business of commercial fishing of sockeyes and pinks, and the attitude of the sport fishermen who are willing to sacrifice all forms of commercial fishing and canning in order to make Puget sound a sportsmen's resort. The strange thing about the situation in the Btate of Washington is that the state supervisor of fisheries clearly shows in the annual reports of his bureau that it is the trollers, not the trap nets, who have in the past taken the major part of the springs and cohoes.
Again we turn to the petition:
There is no truth in the allegation that traps are the only means by which salmon can be taken in our waters in that neighbourhood, as it has been demonstrated that it can be fished by seines, gill nets and trollers, to which the Americans would have no objection as they use the same gear themselves.
It is rather a sinister comment on this, that the hon. member for New Westminster should bring in a bill designed to prohibit the purse seiners from interfering with gill netters at the mouth of the Fraser river. The fact of the matter is, as I have already indicated, that one type of fishermen is continually fighting against the other types.
To continue the quotation:
The above refers to the soekeye run of salmon, but traps are as undesirable as regards the spring and cohoe runs. These fish are heavy in spawn making their way to their spawning ground, swimming in shoals, following the coastline, keeping in shallow water and close inshore, so that they fall an easy prey to the traps, and comparatively few get by.
And yet in 1938 only a trifle over one per cent of the total catch in United States and Canadian waters were taken by traps.
The whole fact of the matter is that it is entirely incorrect to make the statements as made in the petition. The salmon do not hug the shore. They do not run in tight shoals. They come in from the Swiftsure banks some eighteen miles away and swim along the broad line of twelve miles of open water in the strait of Juan de Fuca, and the portion that find themselves on the left hand shore are naturally closed in by the southerly reach of Vancouver island. What other conditions drive them into Puget sound waters I am not in a position to say, but if any member of this house will travel by boat in the daytime from Vancouver to Victoria he will see the amazing

Fisheries Act Amendment

extent to which the fresh waters of the Fraser river penetrate into the salt waters of the strait of Juan de Fuca. It is entirely possible that the fish, recognizing that they are not yet ready for the biological urge that drives them up the fresh water rivers to the spawning grounds, keep away from the fresh water and travel down into the salt water of Puget sound, where there are not many big fresh water rivers. The petition continues:
Traps are the most destructive form of fishing known, as they are open day and night and catch every species of fish, large or small, that comes along whether they happen to be out of season or not. Nothing escapes them or gets through.
And I make this solemn declaration that there is not a single net of any kind that is free from that castigation. The purse seine catches everything it can possibly get hold of. It surrounds every fish within a certain area. Gill netters and all the others do precisely the same thing, and when we talk about immature fish, it has not yet been determined why immature fish run with mature fish. But the fact is that immature fish do run with mature fish, and, doing so, they are bound to be caught with them.
As to the Sooke traps being more destructive, I should like to find out what proportion of fish caught by the trollers leave their jaws on the hooks, having their bodies torn off by the force with which the trollers pass through the water. Trolling is known to-day as the most destructive form of hook-line fishing.
The petition states further:
The abolition of traps would lead to the revival of fishing and employment of many local fishermen as was formerly the case, but who, finding their livelihood gone, have had to find other work, often on relief.
I defy anyone to say that the community of Sooke is a relief community. These people are self-respecting workers and have been for years, many of them owning their own homes, and if every fishing community were like it we should have little relief difficulty in British Columbia.
I could warn the committee about those who act as carriers for this disease I spoke of earlier in my remarks, who consciously or unconsciously infect others, but I sincerely hope the warning is not necessary.
May I read something that has to-day come into my hands. We have been pleaded with to settle this matter, because in Washington they are now sitting to determine whether they should place traps again in the waters of Puget Sound. I quote from the Victoria Times of February 28, and lest anyone should 
wonder how that newspaper of February 28 could reach me to-day I will tell the committee that it was sent by air mail. It reads:
Fish Traps Voted Down in Washington.
Fate of Governor Martin's three fish bills hung in the balance to-day as a result of action of the Washington state legislature late yesterday in voting 69 to 27 to kill house bill 193, permitting return of fishing traps to the Columbia river and Willapa harbour.
The vote on the bill was regarded as a test of the legislators' attitude towards the fish measures and administration leaders to-day refused to say whether they would bring the remaining two bills on to the floor or permit them to "die en route."
Let me quote from Mr. Goodrich:
The state legislature has voted down the first of the three fish trap bills, and the other two will probably never come up at this session at least. The legislature adjourns on March 9 and will not reconvene for two years. We understand that the fact that Canada had five fish traps was deemed of so little importance that it was not even mentioned.
We have heard the plea of the hon. member that it was the one thing that would return 219 traps to Canada. I have proved that the 219 had dwindled down to seventy-five.
The action of the legislature was not a surprise. The purse seiners were well organized as were the sport fishermen, and the trap operators were very much disorganized through jealousies and petty polities.
However, now that the legislature has acted finally it is obvious that nothing Canada does either way will affect the result.
I want to read one word further before I deal with the bill. Mr. Goodrich, criticizing the statement of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, as reported on page 215 of Hansard, has this to say under date of January 30:
As a matter of fact it is safe to say that the minister does not know that the result of continuing to issue our five (not four) trap licences will be to reinstate the pound nets on Puget sound. Indeed, the precise contrary is true. The state of Washington may or may not reinstate this mode of fishing. The purse seiners of course are well organized

This was written long before the statement in the Times of February 28.
-and are opposing the repeal or amendment of initiative No. 77 as they wish to retain the monopoly they have at present of the supply of sockeyes and pinks. However they frankly admit that their catches have dwindled since the abolition of the traps, due to the fact that the fish do not school up as well as they did when the traps were in use. For that reason they are asking permission to build dummy traps in the vicinity of Point Roberts to assist them in making better hauls.
The governor is also much perturbed over the loss sustained by the abolition of the pound nets in the way of loss of employment by fishermen and cannery workers alike.
The director of fisheries finds his department hampered through loss of revenue and is urging amendment to the act.

Fisheries Act Amendment
The cannery men have so far failed to come to any agreement among themselves as to the distribution of the licences in case the pound nets are reestablished.
Sport fishermen are as a rule opposed to all forms of commercial fishing.
It is therefore problematical what action, if any, the legislature will take; but one thing is sure, and this will be apparent to anyone discussing the matter with those most vitally interested, that whatever action they take will be based on what will best serve the interests of the state of Washington and not whether five fish traps at Sooke, B.C., are continued or not.
That I consider to be the crux of the whole situation. We have had plenty of talk about the trade agreement between ourselves and the United States. The United States is entirely justified in looking after its own interest, and Canada is entirely justified in looking after her own interests. If our interests are joint then we have done the right thing in bringing together the international sockeye commission and in being content to rely on their findings. Only by such methods of give and take can we ever reach any satisfactory conclusion on this problem. I say now, without having discussed the matter with anyone, that if it is found that Canada is receiving more than fifty per cent of the fish that come through the strait of Juan de Fuea, then arrangements must be made by which the United States shall get the same quantity as we do, unless they are willing to recognize that the Fraser river is the breeding ground of these fish, and classify the pack accordingly.
Coming to the bill itself, I find that in the seventy-six sections of the Fisheries Act every section is general and common; not a single section is particular and proper. This amendment sought to be placed in the act is a particular amendment. Provisions are made whereby the governor in council and through him the fisheries overseers have power to deal with that act as to administration. Consequently I consider that the essential feature of this amendment is out of order in its application to the general act, and for that reason I am definitely opposed to it. The matter should be left, as it was intended to be left after the finding of the standing committee on fisheries in 1937, at the discretion of the minister. If the minister will use his discretion I am perfectly satisfied. This is a legal business, and just as a department store is able to transact a great deal of business with few people, so in the general apportionment of the industry of the people, one type of fishing is less costly in the way of labour than another. If we are to destroy the fish traps it would be an excellent reason for destroying purse seines and still more for destroying trawlers and gill netters;	and

ultimately we should have to go back to the single hook and line, but for the fact that the sockeye salmon will not take the hook.

speechtext:
I did not'intend to speak on this matter. I had listened to other hon. members from British Columbia who are more familiar with fishing than I am, and who have made an excellent case against the continuance of these fish traps at Sooke. But when I heard the last speaker (Mr. Taylor, Nanaimo) refer to all who oppose fish traps as having contracted some pernicious disease, I decided that I would say a word in opposition to the traps even at the risk of being considered as one who has that disease.
The salmon fisheries of British Columbia are of great importance to that province. They are one of its natural resources. Many years before I went to British Columbia I used to see in the schoolbooks pictures showing that the rivers of British Columbia were teeming with salmon. But that is not the case to-day. A great deal of work and study has been given to the question how best the salmon fisheries in the province can be preserved. Through various causes, sometimes accidental and sometimes arising from ruthless exploitation, the salmon fisheries have been largely depleted. But in recent years vigorous action has been taken to try to re-stock the rivers of British Columbia and to make it easier for the salmon to reach the spawning grounds.
The hon. member for Nanaimo knows a great deal more about fish than I do. I do not know know whether the fish hug the shore or whether they hug anything else; but I do know that the traps at Sooke are so strategically placed as to intercept the greatest number of fish possible.
The hon. member for Nanaimo thinks hon. members may wonder how he got the Victoria Times of February 28 so quickly. He did not tell the committee that Mr. Goodrich, one of the partners in the company that operates the fish traps at Sooke, supplied him with that part of the issue of the Victoria Times. When the hon. member came to this house, I understood him to be representing not the exploiters of labour but the working fishermen who took the fish out of the sea. At that time he was not in such close cooperation with the owners and operators of the fish traps.
All the fishermen in British Columbia are opposed to the fish trap, not because of the fact that it is a trap but because it is an
Fisheries Act Amendment

unfair way of fishing, because it takes an undue share of the fish, and because it operates free from regulations which other fishermen must observe. As a matter of fact, I think it was fairly well substantiated in the marine and fisheries committee a few years ago that employees of the company were appointed as inspectors to see that the rules were observed. I see no reason in the world why this one company should be given an opportunity that is not given any other company or any other individual in the fishing business in British Columbia. If the amount of fish they catch is so small, so insignificant, as the hon. member for Nanaimo would have us believe, that is no argument for keeping the fish traps in operation and fostering envy and hard feelings among the fishermen of British Columbia. Rather it is an additional argument in favour of discontinuing the traps, and I hope the minister will see his way clear to put a halt to a method of fishing which is opposed by ninety per cent of the people of British Columbia.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932   ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OP OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OP FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the importance of this matter is shown by the great interest being taken in it by hon. members representing constituencies in British Columbia. It is a somewhat complicated problem, but it is not a new one. Fish traps, so called, have existed for a long time and have been licensed by the dominion government continuously since 1904. No government and no minister of fisheries has ever wanted to assume the responsibility of exercising the discretion that he has under the Fisheries Act by refusing to grant licences when they were applied for. There are at present, as there have been during that number of years, from three to five licences. These traps which are licensed are stationary fixtures which require quite an investment. I understand that it costs $15,000 to instal each trap, and the people who have been operating these traps and supplying their fish canneries in Victoria have done so for a long period of time and have been successful in placing a superior product on the market.
It may be said that the minister, who has the discretion to refuse or grant the licences, has been protecting the vested interests. I accept either the compliment or the reproach contained in that statement. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) has tried to show that I have changed my mind since assuming the responsibility which I am now discharging. I admit that I have done so. When I came to the department towards the end of 1935, I found that

an agitation had been going on for some time in British Columbia seeking to remove these traps, and that the officials of the department had considered recommending that this be done. Representations were made to me; I looked over the records, and on the representations that were made and the evidence that was before me I thought they were right, so in the early part of 1936 I wrote to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni the letter which he has read this evening and which was before the committee.
In the summer of 1936, however, it was my privilege to visit British Columbia, and I attempted to become acquainted with the problems which existed on that coast, and which were new to me. I studied the various methods of fishing-trolling, purse seining, gill netting and catching fish by means of traps. I walked all over those traps; I covered the whole territory, I believe. I inquired from people in Victoria and Vancouver who I thought were capable of giving advice on the matter, and I found that the agitation arose from competition between those practising the various methods of fishing. Naturally the largest number think they are entitled to rule. The traps are operated by the capitalists, those who have invested, I understand, over a million dollars in an industry which is a credit to the country. They have kept that industry going and have developed around it one of the most creditable villages that can foe found on the coast of British Columbia. I visited that village, which depends entirely upon the fish traps at Sooke. I interviewed the fishermen. I received a delegation from the returned men and another from the wives and daughters of the returned men. I interviewed the clergyman, and after listening to all the representations that could foe made I came back convinced that if that industry were interfered with, the village at Sooke would have to go on relief, because they had no other means of support.
That was in the summer of 1936. When I returned to Ottawa I decided that I could not conscientiously exercise any discretion, but that I must renew the licences for 1937. In 1937 the matter was referred to a committee of this house, and the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) has quoted the recommendations of the committee which have 'been lived up to in every instance. As recommended by the committee, the licence fee has been increased and there has been no increase in the number of licences granted. We have seen that those operating traps shall observe all the regulations, and that no employee of a company operating a trap shall be appointed as supervisor or inspector on the

Fisheries Act Amendment
trap. We have kept in close contact with those interested in these traps and in the conservation, development and preservation of the fishing industry on the Pacific coast. No representations have been made which I thought were sufficient to justify me in changing my mind and refusing to grant from year to year the licences which were applied for.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni has stated that when he made an inquiry in this house not long ago I replied that I had not made up my mind as to what was to be done this year. Of course I had not, because at that time no applications for the renewal of licences had been received. These licences are issued each year, and the decision in the matter is arrived at when applications are before the department. At that time no applications had been received from trap operators, and I had not made up my mind or reached a decision. That goes to show that I am not prejudiced in connection with the issuance of these trap licences.
It has been stated there is grave danger that if we continue to allow traps to be operated, the state of Washington will revert to that method of fishing. That may or may not be so. We have information that the fact that we allow five traps in our waters had no effect whatever on the decision reached on February 28 in the legislature of Washington to turn down the proposal to renew that method of fishing. No representations have been made, either officially or unofficially, by those interested in the state of Washington.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932   ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OP OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OP FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext:
We have been cooperating with the state of Washington. Last year a delegation of representatives of the state of Washington and the government of
the United States came to Ottawa and we had a pleasant conference. No representations were made that we should help them by refusing to grant trap licences for Canadian waters. Not long ago I had occasion to meet officials from the Department of Fisheries in the city of Washington, and no representations were made. Since then this government has appointed a commission known as the International Pacific Salmon Fisheries commission to study the best methods of conservation. One hon. member of this house, the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid), is a member of that commission. The commission is made up of three members from the United States, two of whom I believe, are from the state of Washington, and three Canadians. The commission has already commenced its work of studying the best methods of conserving sockeye.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932   ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OP OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OP FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: Has the commission jurisdiction over the types of gear used in Canadian waters?

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932   ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OP OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OP FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext:
They have no jurisdiction over the types of gear used in Canadian waters, but they can make representations to their respective governments as to what they feel should be done in the matter. No representations have been made as yet by the Canadian commissioners that traps should be removed. The hon. member for New Westminster, speaking as a representative of the fishermen on the Fraser river, has stated that in his opinion these traps should be removed, but the commission as such has not made any representation to the department or to the government. I am sure the work of the commission has not advanced sufficiently to justify it making any such representation.
Further, I understand that the people operating the traps at Sooke have offered every facility to the joint commission to make a study of the effect of these traps on the conservation of our fish in the Fraser river. It has been stated that the removal of these traps would save our fish, but figures speak for themselves. The sockeye is the most valuable salmon on the Pacific coast, and the percentage of sockeye caught last year in the Sooke traps was 1-2 per cent of all the sockeye caught in the Fraser river. The percentage of sockeye caught by Canadian fishermen by other methods of fishing was 54 T per cent, and the percentage caught by fishermen of the state of Washington was 44-7 per cent. There is not much danger that the operation of these traps will cause the destruction of our fish when the percentage of fish caught by that method last year was only 1-2 per cent.
Fisheries Act Amendment

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932   ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OP OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OP FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext: Does that percentage relate to the total pack on the Fraser river or merely to the Canadian pack?

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932   ASSESSMENT UPON OWNERS OP OBSTRUCTIONS TO ASCENT OR DESCENT OP FISH IN STREAMS
speechtext:
The total pack on the Fraser river. My hon. friend will understand that if it referred to the Canadian catch only, the percentage would be practically nil. After all, last season there were only 3,652 cases of sockeye salmon packed from the fish caught in these traps. Looking over the statistics, I find the percentage has not been over five per cent, except in the year 1919, and was varied from six per cent down to one per cent.
I have been told that I should exercise my prerogative and refuse to renew the licences for the operation of the traps this year. But one has only to take into consideration the effect of such action on my part, and then I think hon. gentlemen can well understand why I should hesitate. On the other hand, we have an investment of over one million dollars there made by people who have supported this community for many years. We have a community of good people depending on that industry. We have also the good name of our canned salmon fishery at stake, because these people put up the best grade of goods on the market. Then we have also the right of these people to enjoy their privileges just as other people do.
I feel, Mr. Chairman, on the facts that have been presented so far, that I cannot, just to please one set of fishermen because they are more numerous than another set, take the responsibility that I am being asked to take to-night. I have no personal interest in the matter, nor has the government any. The people who operate these traps are no friends of the government. I am looking at the question purely from the point of view of justice and equity. It is possible that some facts which I have not been able to understand or which have not been placed clearly before the government may exist; but I am sure that no one in this house who does not come from British Columbia and live close to the coast, and who is unfamiliar with the local situation, would take upon himself the responsibility of accepting this evening the amendment suggested by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni and making it the law of the country. I feel that if in the public interest these traps should be removed, more information should be given to members of the house in order to enable them to come to a decision in the matter.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I would suggest that this matter be referred again to the committee on marine and fisheries; and if any

sound reasons be advanced beyond what has already been advanced, there is every disposition on my part and will be on the part of the government to weigh them as carefully as possible. I would accordingly suggest that this bill be not passed in a hurry but be referred to the committee on marine and fisheries where it can be looked into thoroughly, and where every member will have an opportunity to find out the facts upon which to come to a decision in the matter. For that reason I move, Mr. Chairman, that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.

On the last occasion on which this bill was before the house, some objection was taken to a number of clauses beginning with clause 2. The hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Taylor) was not quite satisfied with the definition of "medicine" as found in section
2	(j). The definition as laid down in the section is:
"Medicine" means any substance or mixture of substances that may be used in restoring, correcting or modifying organic functions.
I Mr. J. S. Taylor.]
The hon. member for Nanaimo suggested that we use the word "stimulating" instead of "modifying." The officers of the department and I have had some discussion with him about it, and I understand that he now withdraws his objection to the clause and is prepared to allow it go through as it is.
With respect to paragraph (1), the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) objected to the definition of "manufacture" as meaning "manufacture for sale." On the other hand, the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Matthews) suggested the other night that the word "manufacture" should be used in its fullest dictionary sense. The reason for putting in the definition "manufacture for sale" was to permit persons engaged in scientific research to dispose of their products gratuitously in order that experiments might be carried on. I do not think we could reasonably accept the amendment of the hon. member for Essex East, who suggests that we say "manufacture for sale to the public." That would permit of manufacturers disposing of these articles direct to the medical profession without the department having any control. A large number of products which it is intended to cover by this bill are those which really need some scientific analysis, and medical men generally, particularly in the rural parts of the country, have not at their disposal the apparatus or the laboratories which are necessary for them to assure themselves that the products which they receive for distribution are absolutely non-deleterious. My technical officers advise that it is preferable that the words "manufacture for sale" be kept in the bill.
On the other hand, should I follow the advice of the hon. member for Brandon, who, as is known in this house, is a medical authority of the highest standing, I would strike out altogether "manufacture for sale" and we would be back to the dictionary definition of "manufacture," which would cover a very much wider range than is proposed to be covered by this bill. This bill, I should point out, deals with food, drugs and cosmetics. If we took "manufacture" in its dictionary sense I should be forced to inquire into the gastronomic concoctions which are made in the householder's kitchen, which, after all, would be to some extent a process of manufacture. I might even have to look into the subtle art of mixing cocktails and other concoctions of that kind which, however, pleasant they might be, would perhaps keep the department pretty busy. The first objection to section 5 was in connection with paragraph (j). The objection was raised by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens). This paragraph reads:
Providing for the licensing of manufacturers of cosmetics specifying such terms and conditions as may be deemed advisable in the public interest and prescribing a tariff of fees to be paid for any such licence.
The hon. member for Kootenay East suggested, very properly I think, that there should also be some control over importers. Whatever control we have over Canadian manufacturers should be extended to other manufacturers, and in order to meet his suggestion I have had an amendment prepared, that this paragraph be amended by inserting after the word "cosmetics" in the twenty-ninth line the following:
whether such manufacturers carry on business as such within or without Canada.

Food and Drugs Act

The paragraph would therefore read:
(j) providing for the licensing of manufacturers of cosmetics, whether such manufacturers carry on business as such within or without Canada, specifying such terms and conditions as may be deemed advisable in the public interest and prescribing a tariff of fees to be paid for any such licence.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BROADEN SCOPE AND CLARIFY CERTAIN FEATURES OF THE ACT
speechtext: I move that amendment.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BROADEN SCOPE AND CLARIFY CERTAIN FEATURES OF THE ACT
speechtext: I understand that the minister has an opinion from the Department of Justice. Possibly it is not on the point I am about to raise. I cannot hold up the section unless I raise it here. By that amendment the minister is purporting by order in council to require a foreign subject carrying on business in a foreign country to take out a licence in Canada. Now it is not sale that you are licensing; you are licensing the manufacture. To me it is an unheard of thing for any parliamentary jurisdiction to undertake to do that beyond its own territorial limits. Such a suggestion is anathema to my legal mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BROADEN SCOPE AND CLARIFY CERTAIN FEATURES OF THE ACT
speechtext:
My own opinion was
absolutely that of my hon. friend. I suggested to my officers that we add the word "importers"; in fact that was the suggestion of the hon. member for Kootenay East. But the officers of my department were not quite satisfied with the word "importers" because they feared that some injustice might occur, in that an importer might have a fairly good sized shipment of valuable cosmetics in his possession and for some reason we would turn them down because they had not satisfied all our requirements in regard to health. So they said, "We had better licence the foreign manufacturer." I could not quite agree with that view and suggested that the matter be referred to the Department of Justice. I have received from them a pretty long opinion, which perhaps I had better read into Hansard because, as I say frankly,
I am not quite convinced myself. But as the Department of Justice is the legal adviser to the government and, therefore, to all departments, I suppose I must accept its opinion. The statement reads:
To eliminate any doubt that parliament intended paragraph (j) to extend to manufacturers without as well as within Canada, I would suggest that there be inserted in the paragraph after the word "cosmetics'" the words "whether such manufacturers carry on business as such within or without Canada."
The words of the amendment.
I am given to understand that if the power contained in paragraph (j) set out in section 5 of the bill be given, resultant regulations, following the practice of your department in other similar matters, will require the label attached to the article to carry the licence

number of the manufacturer. If so, any articles
not so labeled will be misbranded within the meaning of the act by virtue of paragraph (g) of section 7 of the act. Section 10(3) prohibits the admission into Canada for use as a food or drug of any article seeking customs entry of import which is reported to be misbranded. I am further given to understand that the close cooperation enjoyed by your department on the part of the customs authorities assures, as far as can be reasonably expected, the prevention of admission into Canada of articles of food or drug misbranded within the meaning of the act.
I may say in passing that we have that close cooperation, and we do check a large number of importations at the border.
I gather from the discussion on pages 830-831 of Hansard-[DOT]
That is the point raised by the hon. member for Kootenay East.
-that those questioning the proposed paragraph desire to see the legislation cover articles of foreign manufacture as adequately as it covers those of domestic manufacture. In my view the proposed authority to license foreign as well as domestic manufacturers of cosmetics coupled with the provisions of the Food and Drugs Act above referred to and the cooperative effort of the customs authorities will not only prevent admission of misbranded goods into Canada but will furnish to the department authority to require and secure information as to ingredients that an importer, other than the manufacturer, is not in a position to give.
So far as power to license foreign manufacturers is concerned, Canada's right to say what shall come into the country indubitably carries with it the power to set down conditions under which a given article shall enter. Consequently I think that adoption of paragraph (j) as set out in section 5 of the bill, changed as above suggested, would vest power in the department to license foreign as well as domestic manufacturers of cosmetics.
That is signed by the acting deputy minister of justice. In face of that opinion I do not think I can do much except propose the amendment which I have proposed.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BROADEN SCOPE AND CLARIFY CERTAIN FEATURES OF THE ACT
speechtext: Does that mean that the foreign manufacturer would apply for a licence?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BROADEN SCOPE AND CLARIFY CERTAIN FEATURES OF THE ACT
speechtext:
He would have to. As a matter of fact, I am informed by the officers of the department that with respect to drugs they very often do. In fact, they even go so far as to allow us to visit their factories. The point is that unless the package is properly branded with the licence number of the manufacturer it could not come in here at all. Apparently the officers of my department and the justice department are satisfied that this will be an effective way to prevent foreign manufacturers or importers from obtaining an advantage in this market, and with that I have to be satisfied.

Food and Drugs Act

speechtext: I speak just from having heard that opinion read once. Down to the last sentence or two I can readily agree with the opinion, and I assume that the minister as a lawyer could also do so, namely, that by a back-handed method you can force a foreign manufacturer to come to you of his own volition and ask for a licence. But that opinion winds up by saying that by putting those words in that paragraph of this act you vest in the department power to license a foreign manufacturer.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BROADEN SCOPE AND CLARIFY CERTAIN FEATURES OF THE ACT
speechtext: It does not quite say that.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BROADEN SCOPE AND CLARIFY CERTAIN FEATURES OF THE ACT
speechtext: Even though it be the opinion of the Department of Justice, with great respect I wish to record my disagreement with that opinion, because I dislike to see something going on our statute books which I am firmly convinced will not stand up in the courts.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BROADEN SCOPE AND CLARIFY CERTAIN FEATURES OF THE ACT
speechtext: The criterion, I suppose, is that they think it is going to work.
