speechtext: Go ahead.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BROADEN SCOPE AND CLARIFY CERTAIN FEATURES OF THE ACT
speechtext: What I am getting at is that, as the minister said, quite a number of letters of protest were received in regard to the extraordinarily wide powers-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BROADEN SCOPE AND CLARIFY CERTAIN FEATURES OF THE ACT
speechtext: That is under paragraphs (k) and (m).

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BROADEN SCOPE AND CLARIFY CERTAIN FEATURES OF THE ACT
speechtext: I was going to ask the minister, when we come to them, to tell us his views in connection with that matter and whether he proposes any changes by reason of those representations.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BROADEN SCOPE AND CLARIFY CERTAIN FEATURES OF THE ACT
speechtext:
I do; I am now about to move an amendment. I will read one of the letters, which is the type of letter sent; they were nearly all the same. It says:
Paragraph (k) gives the governor in council the power to make regulations "prohibiting the sale or defining the conditions of sale of any substance . . . etcetera." Now since the adjective "any" is used, regulations could at any time be passed by orders in council pro-71492-96J
hibiting the sale of a substance which is quite harmless, just as one could when it is dangerous.
The explanatory notes accompanying this section give as the reason for this inclusion in the bill "certain substances .	.	. may be
dangerous to life." We therefore desire that the words "dangerous to life" be inserted immediately following the word "substance" in this paragraph, or if preferred, "deleterious to health" could be inserted.
I am not proposing to insert the words "dangerous to life" except perhaps in conjunction with something else. I might be obliged to go to the graveyard to prove my ease, and I do not want to wait until someone is dead in order to be able to say a substance is dangerous to life, but the amendment I am proposing would be "which may be injurious to health when used as a food or drug," which will come to the same thing. If any hon. member wished to insist on the words "dangerous to life" I could add them, but it would not be of much value. But I must at least keep the words "injurious to health." It would be impossible to operate the act as efficiently as we should like if the criterion were to be that something was dangerous to life, as that would be difficult to prove in any court unless someone actually died, and I do not think it is the intention of this committee that we should allow the manufacturers of these products to go ahead making guinea-pigs of the people of Canada until a fatality occurs. So I think, by the amendment which I have asked my colleague to move, I have met the objections which have been suggested; in fact I have practically adopted the phraseology suggested in all these letters.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BROADEN SCOPE AND CLARIFY CERTAIN FEATURES OF THE ACT
speechtext: "Injurious to health" seems satisfactory.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BROADEN SCOPE AND CLARIFY CERTAIN FEATURES OF THE ACT
speechtext:
It seems as good as "deleterious to health." So I would ask my colleague to move that paragraph (k) be amended by inserting after the word "substance" in the thirty-fourth line thereof the words "which may be injurious to health when used." The section would then read:
(k) prohibiting the sale or defining the conditions of sale of any substance which may be injurious to health when used as a food or drug or restricting in like manner its use as an ingredient in the manufacture of food or drug;

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BROADEN SCOPE AND CLARIFY CERTAIN FEATURES OF THE ACT
speechtext: I so move.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BROADEN SCOPE AND CLARIFY CERTAIN FEATURES OF THE ACT
speechtext: Why say "may be injurious?" Why not be definite?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BROADEN SCOPE AND CLARIFY CERTAIN FEATURES OF THE ACT
speechtext:
There are many things about which we are not quite sure. Since I have not my technical advisers before me, perhaps my hon. friend the leader of the opposition
Food and Drugs Act

(Mr. Manion) would tell me if I am right in my medical terms, but I think there was a glycol substance which we refused someone the right to use in flavouring extracts because we feared it might be injurious. While negotiations were going on and I was being bombarded with representations about it, two people, one in Nova Scotia and one somewhere else, died as a consequence of using this substance. Well, at the time the officers of the department were not in a position to prove that this substance was injurious, but the deaths indicated it definitely was. I think we should be given some leeway, because with the advance of science we cannot say definitely that these substances are dangerous, but we may have reason to suspect that they are.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BROADEN SCOPE AND CLARIFY CERTAIN FEATURES OF THE ACT
speechtext:
I think that is true; I
think the matter should be left open.

speechtext:

You say "a substance which may be injurious to health." Why not say "a substance that is injurious to health"? Some substance might be injurious in one instance and not injurious in another.

speechtext:
Is that not the very
reason why there must be. some discretion left with the officials? This section merely gives power to prohibit by order in council the use of something which may be injurious to health. In other words, they may wish to prohibit the use of this glycol product in an edible food and not prohibit it in something else.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BROADEN SCOPE AND CLARIFY CERTAIN FEATURES OF THE ACT
speechtext: In antifreeze, for instance.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BROADEN SCOPE AND CLARIFY CERTAIN FEATURES OF THE ACT
speechtext:
I think we have to leave
them some discretion.
